name: Four Noble Truths
desc:
The overarching framework of the Buddhist problematic, and the content of the Buddha's first turning of the wheel of the Dharma. The four truths are not four truths standing side by side but a single chain running from diagnosis to cure: [[dukkha|the truth of suffering]] points out the unsatisfactoriness and oppressiveness of existence; [[samudaya|the truth of origin]] traces the conditions from which that unsatisfactoriness arises; the truth of cessation confirms that those conditions can be brought to a complete end; and the truth of the path gives the concrete method for that ending. Its form approximates the structure of medical diagnosis and treatment — knowing the disease, knowing its cause, knowing it can be cured, knowing the remedy.

The four truths are linked to one another by cause and effect: suffering is the result and origin the cause, cessation is the result and the path the cause. The first two truths explain how the round of rebirth comes about, the latter two how its cessation is possible; the four truths are therefore at once a theory of saṃsāra and a theory of liberation.

“Noble” (ārya) here does not mean “sacred and beyond doubt” but “comprehended by the noble ones,” that is, what is realised at the stage of seeing the path. The four truths are also the doctrinal basis that all Buddhist schools accept in common and dispute least — however later systems of doctrinal classification drew their divisions, they all placed the four truths first.

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicle 15, sūtra 379, “Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma”
src.q: “There are the [[four_truths|four noble truths]]. What are the four? They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”
First delivered by the Buddha to the five monks at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī; the Chinese and Pali transmissions correspond in content.

src.t: Tang dynasty, trans. Yijing, *Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Wheel of the Dharma* (San Zhuan Falun Jing) (Taishō Tripiṭaka, vol. 2)
src.q: A separate variant translation setting out the doctrine of the three turnings of the four truths.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (first delivered at the Deer Park after the Buddha's awakening)
tt.fix: c. 3rd century BCE (systematically arranged in Abhidharma treatises as the four truths and their sixteen aspects)
tt.trans: Liu-Song dynasty, trans. Guṇabhadra, *Saṃyukta-āgama* (c. 435–443); Tang dynasty, trans. Yijing, *Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Wheel of the Dharma* (700–711)

name: The Truth of Suffering
desc:
The unsatisfactoriness and oppressiveness of existence. The literal sense of *duḥkha* is connected with a wheel whose axle is off-centre and which therefore turns unsteadily; by extension it means what cannot be borne, the incomplete, the not-at-ease.

The scriptures set it out as the eight kinds of suffering: birth, ageing, sickness, death, separation from what is loved, association with what is hated, not obtaining what is sought, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. The treatises more often summarise them as the three kinds of suffering — the suffering of pain (painful feeling is itself suffering), the suffering of change (pleasant feeling is suffering when it turns), and the suffering inherent in conditioned formation (all [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]] flow on moment by moment and are not subject to one's control, which is the most fundamental form of suffering).

These enumerations do not assert that life is nothing but pain; they point out that whatever arises from causes and conditions cannot escape change and lack of mastery. The truth of suffering is therefore “observation as it really is” (yathābhūta), and is quite different from emotional pessimism.

src.t: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.11, “Discourse on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma” (Southern transmission; the Chinese counterpart is An Shigao’s *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma*)
src.q: “The noble truth of suffering is this: the suffering of birth, the suffering of ageing, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, sorrow, anxiety and distress, the suffering of encountering the hateful, the suffering of separation from the loved, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought — in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.”
Subsumes all suffering under the three kinds of suffering: the suffering of pain, the suffering of change and the suffering inherent in conditioned formation.

tt.fix: The doctrine of the three kinds of suffering appears in Sarvāstivāda treatises; the eight kinds of suffering were fixed in the Chinese Āgamas and in scholastic commentary

name: The Truth of the Origin of Suffering
desc:
The arising, root and bringing about of result of suffering. The Sanskrit *samudaya* = sam (together, in combination) + udaya (arising, coming forth); it means arising together, origination, the bringing about of result, and root, and not “a collection” in the sense of the modern Chinese word.

The specific content of the truth of origin is explicitly defined in the scriptures as [[craving|craving]]: the craving that leads to further rebirth, that is accompanied by delight and greed, that takes delight here and there. It is divided into craving for sense-desires (the craving for sensual pleasure), craving for existence (the craving for continued being), and craving for non-existence (the craving for annihilation). The treatises give a more fundamental account by way of [[ignorance|ignorance]] and the afflictions (fetters and proclivities).

The truth of origin is therefore not an abstract “cause” but a set of observable, terminable psychological forces: craving presupposes ignorance, has “feeling” as its direct condition, and from it the cyclical structure of “affliction–karma–suffering” is drawn out.

src.t: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.11, “Discourse on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma” (Southern transmission)
src.q: “The noble truth of the origin of suffering is this: the [[craving|craving]] that brings about further existence, that is accompanied by delight and greed, that takes delight here and there — namely, craving for sense-desires, craving for existence, craving for non-existence.”
Takes [[ignorance|ignorance]] as the root of the truth of origin, and explains the arising of suffering through the two kinds of origin, affliction and karma.

tt.fix: Scholastic treatises of the schools reorganised the content of the truth of origin as affliction–karma–suffering

name: The Truth of Cessation
desc:
Suffering can cease, and that cessation is [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]]. The standard scriptural formulation is: “the complete fading away and cessation of this [[craving|craving]], its abandonment, relinquishment, release, with no lingering attachment” — what ceases is not some entity but the entire set of conditions for craving, utterly undone.

The truth of cessation is thus a negative proposition about conditions: when the conditions that produce suffering no longer exist, suffering cannot arise. It is not “destroying suffering” but “suffering no longer being produced.”

The same thing bears different names in different systems: in the three seals it is “the peace of nirvāṇa,” among the unconditioned dharmas it is analytical cessation, the unconditioned (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), and in the four truths it is the truth of cessation. Different names, one referent.

src.t: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.11, “Discourse on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma” (Southern transmission)
src.q: “The noble truth of the cessation of suffering is this: the complete fading away and cessation of this [[craving|craving]], its abandonment, relinquishment, release, with no lingering attachment.”
Cessation through discernment, the unconditioned — “discernment” means the discriminating examination of the four truths; the cessation realised through the discernment of wisdom.

tt.fix: The scholastic location of “cessation through discernment, the unconditioned” was established gradually between c. 2nd century BCE and the 4th century CE

name: The Truth of the Path
desc:
The method for ending suffering, which the scriptures set out directly as the [[eightfold|noble eightfold path]]. The first characteristic of the truth of the path is that it is defined as the “middle way”: the [[doc_15|Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma]] (Zhuan Falun Jing) says at the outset that one who has gone forth should not approach either extreme — the one being attachment to sense-desires (base, vulgar, the practice of ordinary people, not noble, unprofitable), the other being self-mortifying asceticism (painful, not noble, unprofitable). What awakens to full enlightenment on avoiding these two extremes is the eightfold path.

The eightfold path can be subsumed under the three trainings in ethics, concentration and wisdom: [[right_speech|right speech]], right action and right livelihood belong to the training in ethics; right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration belong to the training in concentration; right view and right thought belong to the training in wisdom. This subsumption is the standard classification used by later treatises in arranging the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment.

The “path” of the truth of the path is what is to be cultivated (bhāvanā), as against the “realisation” of the truth of cessation, the “abandonment” of the truth of origin and the “understanding” of the truth of suffering, constituting the four tasks: understanding suffering, abandoning its origin, realising its cessation, cultivating the path.

src.t: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.11, “Discourse on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma” (Southern transmission; the “two extremes” and “middle way” passage also appears in An Shigao’s translation)
src.q: “Monks, there are two extremes that one who has gone forth should not practise … not entering these two extremes, the middle way that produces vision and knowledge has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]] … namely, this noble eightfold path.”
The same passage; the Pali version has “the middle way” (majjhimā paṭipadā).

tt.fix: The subsumption under the three trainings appears in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 25, and other treatises

name: The Noble Eightfold Path
desc:
[[right_view|Right view]], [[right_thought|right thought]], right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. The eight factors are not eight successive stages but the simultaneous unfolding of one and the same practice at the levels of cognition, speech, conduct, livelihood, mental effort, awareness and meditative concentration; the treatises call this “concurrence at a single moment.”

The first two factors belong to the training in wisdom, the middle three to the training in ethics, and the last three to the training in concentration. Right view stands first because if one's knowledge and views are incorrect, all the subsequent factors become wrong paths; but right view itself is not a purely theoretical acceptance — it is “knowing and seeing the four truths and dependent origination as they really are,” repeatedly verified in actual contemplation.

The eightfold path is the hub of the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, and every later school, whether it teaches sudden or gradual awakening, has to account for its place — the Chan teaching of “pointing directly at the human mind” is one instance of not proceeding by the successive stages beginning with right view.

src.q: “Namely: [[right_view|right view]], right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.”
The latter gives an extended, factor-by-factor exposition of the [[eightfold|noble eightfold path]], explaining the accompanying factors of right concentration and their sequence.

tt.fix: The extended exposition of each factor appears in *Majjhima-nikāya* 117; the scholastic arrangement in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 25

name: Right View
desc: Knowing and seeing the four truths, [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] and causality as they really are; it is the forerunner of the whole of practice. The scriptures divide right view into two kinds: mundane right view (believing that there is cause and effect, good and evil, karmic retribution) and supramundane right view (knowing the four truths, realising the undefiled). The former is the basis of the latter; without the former all wholesome conduct loses its ground.

src.q: Defines [[right_view|right view]] as “knowing suffering, knowing the origin of suffering, knowing the cessation of suffering, knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”
Takes “knowing the [[four_truths|four noble truths]]” as right view.

tt.fix: The distinction between mundane and supramundane right view appears in *Majjhima-nikāya* 117 and in the treatises

name: Right Thought
desc: Also rendered right resolve or right intention. It refers to three intentions: renunciation (freedom from desire), non-ill-will, and harmlessness. Their opposites are the thought of desire, the thought of ill-will and the thought of harm. Right thought stands after [[right_view|right view]] — once the view is established, the orientation of the mind turns accordingly; it belongs to the purification of mental action.

src.q: “The thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill-will, the thought of harmlessness.”

name: Right Speech
desc: Abstention from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech and from idle chatter — the four items of the ten wholesome courses of action that concern verbal action. Within the [[eightfold|noble eightfold path]], right speech belongs to the training in ethics, and its criterion is not only “what was said” but also “whether it is timely, whether it is true, whether it is beneficial, whether it is kindly.”

src.q: “Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter.”

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicle 33 (concerning the five precepts)
src.q: The four items concerning verbal action in the [[ten_paths|ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses of action]] correspond to these.

name: Right Action
desc: Abstention from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from sexual misconduct; guarding bodily action. These coincide with the first three of the [[five_precepts|five precepts]]. The treatises classify these three as “precepts by nature” — because they are in themselves real offences regardless of circumstance, unlike the precept against drinking alcohol, which is a “precept of prohibition.”

src.q: “Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct.”

“Of the lay follower's [[five_precepts|five precepts]], how many are real offences and how many are offences of prohibition? Answer: four are real offences; the one precept against drinking alcohol is an offence of prohibition.”

tt.fix: The distinction between precepts by nature and precepts of prohibition appears in Sarvāstivāda Vinaya literature

name: Right Livelihood
desc:
To earn a living in a way that does not harm living beings. Right livelihood has a special place within the [[sila|training in ethics]]: in the first seven factors, what [[right_speech|right speech]] and right action govern is “what has already been done,” whereas what right livelihood governs is “by what means one lives” — that is, it extends the regulation of conduct forward to the whole manner of sustaining life.

**Wrong livelihood** (mithyā-ājīva) is illustrated differently in the northern and southern transmissions, and the two must be kept apart:

- **The five kinds of wrong livelihood for those who have gone forth** — according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da Zhidu Lun), fascicle 19, and the *Yogācārabhūmi* (Yujia Shi Di Lun): feigning what is extraordinary, proclaiming one's own virtues, practising divination of good and ill fortune, raising one's voice to display authority, and speaking in order to obtain offerings. All five point to one thing: exchanging the status of a renunciant for material gain.
- **Occupations the lay follower should not engage in** — according to the *Aṅguttara-nikāya* (Zengzhi Bu) 5.177 and others: trading in weapons, trading in human beings, trading in meat, trading in liquor, trading in poison. The scriptures call these “occupations that should not be engaged in” and do not name them “wrong livelihood” — lay followers do not live by “teaching the Dharma in exchange for offerings,” so the five kinds of wrong livelihood given in the treatises do not apply to them.

What the two accounts share lies in the **criterion**, not in the items: what right livelihood asks is not “what is forbidden” but “whether this way of earning a living is constituted on the condition of harming living beings.” Thus trafficking in drugs, in human beings or in weapons is listed as a forbidden zone for lay followers because its profit is directly founded on harm to living beings, not because the trade itself is “impure.”

Right livelihood extends practice from the taming of the mind to the manner of social subsistence; it is the most social branch of the training in ethics, and the only one of the precepts undertaken by lay followers that directly regulates their economic life.

src.q: “Abandoning wrong livelihood, one lives by [[right_livelihood|right livelihood]].”
Sets out the five kinds of wrong livelihood in detail.

src.t: *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.177, “The Five Things Not to Be Sold” (the Chinese counterpart is the sūtra on “means of livelihood” in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*)
src.q: “A lay follower possessed of five qualities should not engage in five trades: trading in weapons, trading in human beings, trading in meat, trading in liquor, trading in poison.”

Takes [[right_livelihood|right livelihood]] to be “the purification of the three actions of body, speech and mind,” and, together with right speech and right action, as comprised within the training in ethics.

tt.fix: The classification of the five kinds of wrong livelihood for renunciants was fixed in the treatises (c. 2nd–5th century); the five occupations the lay follower should not engage in appear in *Aṅguttara-nikāya* 5.177 and the Chinese Āgamas

name: Right Effort
desc: Also called the four right exertions: to abandon evil that has arisen; to prevent the arising of evil not yet arisen; to bring about the arising of good not yet arisen; and to increase good that has arisen. Of the four, the first two are protective and the latter two productive. Right effort is repeatedly stressed among the [[thirty_seven_bodhipakkhiya|thirty-seven aids to enlightenment]], because no contemplation can do without the element of sustained exertion.

src.q: “For the non-arising of evil not yet arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, rouses energy, applies the mind and sustains the mind …”

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicle 26 (sūtras on the four right exertions)
src.q: The fixed formulation of the four right exertions.

name: Right Mindfulness
desc: Clearly remembering and not forgetting in regard to the four objects — body, feelings, mind and dharmas — that is, the practice of the [[four_foundations|the four establishments of mindfulness]]. Right mindfulness is not “remembering things” but continuous awareness of the bodily and mental processes of the present — the treatises explain “mindfulness” as “not losing the object of contemplation.” the four establishments of mindfulness counter the four inversions of permanence, pleasure, self and purity by contemplating the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent and dharmas as non-self.

src.q: “This is the one way that purifies beings, transcends grief and lamentation, extinguishes pain and sorrow, reaches the method, and realises [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]]: namely, the four establishments of mindfulness.”

src.t: *Madhyama-āgama* (Zhong Ahan Jing), fascicle 24, sūtra 98, “Satipaṭṭhāna Sūtra” (Nianchu Jing)
src.q: The corresponding Chinese translation, belonging to the recitational tradition of the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda school]].

tt.fix: Pali *Dīgha-nikāya* 22 and the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* 98 are the fixed texts of two distinct lineages

name: Right Concentration
desc: One-pointedness of mind, namely the [[four_dhyanas|four dhyānas and eight concentrations]] and the like; it is the power of concentration on which contemplative wisdom depends. The scriptures stress that right concentration is only called “right” when it arises together with the other seven factors — if there is absorption alone without right view and right mindfulness, it is a mundane concentration that can lead to rebirth in the heavens but does not escape birth and death. The treatises therefore distinguish “mundane concentration” from “supramundane concentration.”

src.q: Explains [[right_samadhi|right concentration]] by way of the four dhyānas and enumerates its accompanying factors.
The locus at which the classic description of the four dhyānas was fixed.

tt.fix: The description of the four dhyānas was fixed in sūtras of the *Sāmaññaphala* type; the detailed scholastic exposition appears in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 28

name: Craving
desc:
The three kinds — craving for sense-desires, craving for existence and craving for non-existence — are the core dynamic of the [[samudaya|truth of origin]] and the eighth link, “craving,” of [[twelve_links|the twelve links of dependent origination]]. The division into three covers the whole range of life's pursuits: the pursuit of sensory pleasure, the pursuit of continued existence, and the pursuit of total annihilation.

The mark of craving is not “liking” but “repetitive pursuit driven by a sense of insufficiency” — even when the desired object has been obtained, it immediately turns to the next one. Hence it is placed after “feeling” in the twelve links of dependent origination: when the three feelings of pain, pleasure and neutrality arise, craving arises along with them.

src.q: “Namely: craving for sense-desires, craving for existence, craving for non-existence.”

name: Ignorance
desc:
The not-knowing of the four truths, [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] and [[anatta|non-self]]. It is at once the root of the truth of origin and the first link of the twelve links of dependent origination, and thus the starting point of the whole round of rebirth.

Ignorance is not “a lack of knowledge” but “a distortion of the mode of cognition itself” — grasping the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, and suffering as pleasure. Ignorance can therefore only be countered by “knowledge” (vijjā), that is, replaced by directly realised wisdom; it cannot be removed by accumulating conceptual knowledge. This is also why ignorance appears both at the beginning of practice (as the affliction to be abandoned) and at its end (as the knowledge to be transformed into).

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicle 12 (sūtras of the nidāna-saṃyutta)
src.q: “That one is without knowledge, without insight; one does not know form as it really is, does not know feeling, perception, formations or consciousness as they really are — this is called [[ignorance|ignorance]].”
Ignorance stands first among the links of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]].

name: The Structure of Diagnosis and Cure
desc:
The logical form of the four truths: diagnosis (suffering) → aetiology (origin) → possibility of cure (cessation) → treatment plan (path). This structure is often compared to a physician treating an illness, and it is the most methodological part of Buddhist theory.

Its importance lies in this: what the four truths give is not a cosmology but a “problem–solution” procedure. The reason later [[panjiao|doctrinal classification]] could assign different scriptures to different positions is precisely that they can be seen as partial unfoldings of this procedure.

src.q: The four tasks stated in the sūtra — “suffering is to be understood, its origin is to be abandoned, its cessation is to be realised, the path is to be cultivated” — are the classic formulation of this structure.
Compares a skilled physician with the four truths.

name: All Formations Are Suffering
desc:
Whatever is made by causes and conditions is unstable and cannot be relied upon, and is therefore suffering. Here “formation” (saṅkhāra) means the same as the “formation” in “[[impermanence|all formations are impermanent]],” namely all [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]], and not feelings alone.

**The three kinds of suffering** are its standard unfolding:

- **The suffering of pain** — painful feeling is itself suffering (sickness, pain, grief and distress);
- **The suffering of change** — pleasant feeling will in the end turn, and in turning it is suffering (so pleasant feeling is not the opposite of suffering but a mitigated form of it);
- **The suffering inherent in conditioned formation** — all conditioned dharmas flow on moment by moment, driven by karma and affliction, and are not subject to one's own control; this is the most fundamental form of suffering.

“All formations are suffering” is therefore not an emotional judgement of pessimism but a definition of the mode of existence that is “conditioned formation”: **because impermanent, therefore suffering** — precisely because they arise and perish in every moment and cannot be mastered, all formations are said to be suffering. Together with “all formations are impermanent” and “all [[anatta|dharmas are without self]],” this item makes up the **three characteristics** (tilakkhaṇa) of the southern transmission, the object of the insight knowledges of the Theravāda; the Chinese transmission's [[four_seals|four seals of the Dharma]] instead take this item into the seal, placing it alongside impermanence, non-self and the peace of nirvāṇa.

The doctrinal sequence is: because impermanent, therefore suffering; because suffering, therefore non-self — the three are not three coordinate conclusions but three faces of one and the same observation.

src.t: *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 3.136; *Dhammapada* verse 278 (the fixed phrasing of the three characteristics)
src.q: “[[impermanence|All formations are impermanent]], all formations are suffering, all dharmas are without self.” — the standard formulation of the three characteristics in the southern transmission.
In the contemplation of feeling, one contemplates the three feelings as all suffering; also the passage on “contemplating arising and perishing.”
Subsumes all suffering under the suffering of pain, the suffering of change and the suffering inherent in conditioned formation.
Takes the three characteristics as the object of the insight knowledges, with the sixteen insight knowledges unfolding in sequence.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (one of the three characteristics)
tt.fix: The systematic classification of the three kinds of suffering appears in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 22 (4th–5th century); the southern transmission's taking of the three characteristics as the object of insight is found in the *Visuddhimagga* (5th century)

rel.dukkha: the aspect of the truth of suffering
rel.southern_tradition: the three characteristics as the object of insight

name: The Three Seals of the Dharma
desc:
The criterion for determining what is and is not the Dharma: [[impermanence|all formations are impermanent]], [[nonself_seal|all dharmas are without self]], and the peace of nirvāṇa. Whatever contradicts these three is not accepted as the Buddha's Dharma. “Seal” (mudrā) means a stamp or a seal — as Puguang's *Notes on the Abhidharmakośa* (Jushe lun ji) says: “If it accords with this seal, it is a Buddhist scripture; if it contradicts this seal, it is not the Buddha's word.”

There is a question of textual strata here that is often overlooked: the content of the three phrases first appears in *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing) sūtra no. 262, but that sūtra merely records that Ānanda taught these three phrases to Channa, and does not call them a “dharma seal.” The earliest juxtaposition of the three phrases under the name “three seals of the Dharma” can be traced to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Genben Shuo Yiqie Youbu Pinaye) and to the *Abhidharma-dharma-skandha-pāda-śāstra* (Apidamo Fayun Zu Lun), “Chapter on Dependent Origination”; Nāgārjuna's *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da Zhidu Lun), fascicle 15, likewise places the three side by side and says, “Because one has obtained the seal of the Buddha's Dharma, one penetrates without obstruction, as one who has obtained the king's seal meets no hindrance.” Master Yinshun held that the three seals of the Dharma developed out of the “three samādhis.”

The Theravāda of the southern transmission has a closely similar concept called the “three characteristics” (tilakkhaṇa): all formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all dharmas are without self — although the *Visuddhimagga* (Qingjing Daolun) possesses their substantive content, it does not establish the name “dharma seal.” It may therefore be said that the fixed name “three seals of the Dharma” was gathered and transmitted by the Sarvāstivāda alone, and afterwards became the settled conclusion of the sectarian schools and of the northern Mahāyāna.

src.q: “The monks said to Channa: ‘Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, formations and consciousness are impermanent; all formations are impermanent; all [[nonself_seal|dharmas are without self]]; nirvāṇa is peace.’” — the earliest scripture in which the three phrases stand together, though it does not give them the name “dharma seal.”

src.t: *Abhidharma-dharma-skandha-pāda-śāstra* (Fayun Zu Lun), fascicle 12, “Chapter on Dependent Origination”
src.q: Trans. Xuanzang: “Regarding the [[three_seals|three seals of the Dharma]] one gives rise to doubt: Are all formations impermanent, or are not all formations impermanent? Are all dharmas non-self? … Is nirvāṇa peace, or is nirvāṇa not peace?” — one of the sources for the fixed name “three seals of the Dharma.”

“The Blessed One then taught the Dharma in three phrases, saying: Bhadra, all formations are impermanent, all dharmas are [[anatta|non-self]], and there is the peace of nirvāṇa; one thereby realises the true reality of all dharmas. This is called the three seals of the Dharma.”

Brings together the seal of impermanence of all produced, conditioned dharmas, the seal of non-self of all dharmas, and the seal of the Dharma of the true reality of nirvāṇa, under the name of the three kinds of dharma seal.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the content of the three phrases)
tt.fix: c. 2nd–1st century BCE (the name “three seals of the Dharma” was fixed in the Sarvāstivāda *Dharma-skandha-pāda* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*)
tt.trans: Liu-Song dynasty, trans. Guṇabhadra, *Saṃyukta-āgama* (fascicle 10, sūtra no. 262); Tang dynasty, trans. Xuanzang, *Dharma-skandha-pāda* (659); Yao-Qin dynasty, trans. Kumārajīva, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (402–405)

name: All Formations Are Impermanent
desc:
All [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]] arise and perish in every moment; not one of them abides permanently. “Formation” (saṃskāra) here means what is fabricated, conditioned existence, including matter, mind and mental factors, and even such “formations dissociated from mind” as time and concepts.

Impermanence has two levels: impermanence over a period (the arising, abiding, changing and perishing of things on a longer timescale, such as a person's birth and death) and moment-by-moment impermanence (arising and perishing in every instant, with no momentary abiding). The treatises take moment-by-moment impermanence as the more fundamental level — because impermanence over a period is only the surface appearance accumulated out of moment-by-moment impermanence.

src.q: “All formations are impermanent.”
Explains the impermanence of [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]] through the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing and perishing, and discusses the meaning of perishing in every moment.

tt.fix: The theoretical account of moment-by-moment impermanence appears in Sarvāstivāda treatises

name: All Dharmas Are Non-Self
desc:
All dharmas — whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether the world of sentient beings or the material world — lack an independent, unchanging, self-existent nature. “Self” (ātman) has a determinate meaning in the Indian context: only that which possesses all four senses — permanent (unchanging), one (independent), master (self-existent) and sovereign (controlling) — is called a “self.” The Buddhist [[anatta|non-self]] denies that any dharma possesses any one of these four senses.

Non-self is therefore not the nihilistic assertion “I do not exist” but “no dharma possesses the substantially real character of being permanent, one and sovereign.” This formulation is continuous with “emptiness”: emptiness is non-self, non-self is emptiness.

src.q: “All [[nonself_seal|dharmas are without self]].”
“Whatever form there is, whether past, whether future, whether present … all of it is to be observed as it really is as not self and not belonging to a self.”

name: The Peace of Nirvāṇa
desc:
The cessation of suffering, the stilling of the [[continuity|continuum]]. In the three seals it appears as “the peace of nirvāṇa,” in the four truths it is the truth of cessation, and among the unconditioned dharmas it is analytical cessation, the unconditioned (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

Nirvāṇa is not “a place” or “a state” but the cessation of greed, hatred and delusion itself. The treatises divide nirvāṇa into two: nirvāṇa with a remainder of substratum (the afflictions are already cut off, but the body of the five aggregates remains) and nirvāṇa without a remainder of substratum (the continuum of the five aggregates also comes to an end). The Mahāyāna establishes in addition “non-abiding nirvāṇa” — not abiding in saṃsāra, yet not abiding in nirvāṇa either, not forsaking sentient beings because of the vow of compassion.

src.q: “[[nirvana|Nirvāṇa]] is peace.”
“The true reality of all dharmas is the city of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]], and the city has three gates: emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness.”

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: “Without relying on the conventional truth, the ultimate meaning is not attained; without attaining the ultimate meaning, [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]] is not attained.”

tt.fix: The distinction between nirvāṇa with and without a remainder of substratum, and non-abiding nirvāṇa, appear in the treatises of the schools and in Mahāyāna śāstras

rel.nirodha: that is, the truth of cessation
rel.unconditioned: that is, cessation through discernment, the unconditioned

name: The Four Seals of the Dharma
desc:
The [[three_seals|three seals of the Dharma]] plus “[[all_suffering|all feelings are suffering]]” (or “all formations are suffering”) make the four seals of the Dharma. Their source is the *Ekottarika-āgama* (Zeng Yi Ahan Jing) — that sūtra calls “all formations are entirely impermanent, all formations are suffering, all formations are non-self, nirvāṇa is eternal peace” the “four bases of the Dharma.” The *Yogācārabhūmi* (Yujia Shi Di Lun) calls them the “four dharma-udānas” (the summary headings of the Dharma).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da Zhidu Lun) records another set of four dharma seals, taking impermanence, non-self, signlessness and the peace of nirvāṇa as the four. The Mahāyāna further establishes a single “seal of the true reality”: the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, “Expedient Means” chapter, speaks of the “seal of the true reality,” and Zhiyi of Tiantai, in the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), takes the true reality of all dharmas as the single seal of the true reality, as the Mahāyāna criterion.

“All feelings are suffering” among the four seals corresponds directly to the truth of suffering in the four truths — “all feelings are suffering” is the unfolding of “in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging” in the truth of suffering. The four seals are thus in fact the point of junction between the three seals and the four truths.

src.q: “All formations are entirely impermanent, all formations are suffering, all formations are [[anatta|non-self]], nirvāṇa is eternal peace” — called the “four bases of the Dharma.”
Calls these four the “four dharma-udānas,” and says that Buddhas and bodhisattvas teach them in reliance on the [[three_doors|three doors of liberation]] in order to purify sentient beings.
The “seal of the true reality”; Zhiyi's *[[doc_33|Fahua Xuanyi]]* takes the true reality of all dharmas as the single seal of the true reality.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the three dharma phrases) – period of the compilation of the Ekottarika-āgama (3rd–1st century BCE)
tt.fix: The *Ekottarika-āgama* establishes the “four bases of the Dharma”; the *Yogācārabhūmi* establishes the “four dharma-udānas”

rel.dukkha: all feelings are suffering is the truth of suffering

name: Non-Self
desc:
No dharma has an independent, unchanging, self-existent nature. Non-self is not “I do not exist” but “there is no substantially real self.”

“Self” (ātman) has a determinate meaning in the Indian context: the four senses of permanent (ever unchanging), one (independent, not depending on another), master (autonomous) and sovereign (controlling). The Buddhist non-self denies that any dharma possesses these four senses.

There are two paths of argument for non-self:
- The analytical: experience is analysed by way of the [[five_aggregates|five aggregates]], the [[twelve_ayatana|twelve sense bases]] and the eighteen elements, and no dharma answering to “self” is found among them (the five aggregates are not self);
- The inferential: whatever is impermanent is suffering, and whatever is suffering is not self and does not belong to a self — “because impermanent, therefore suffering; because suffering, therefore non-self.”

In early Buddhism, non-self has both a practical and a theoretical side: practically, it serves to remove self-grasping and to prevent the expansion of self-consciousness, and is a criterion of ethical practice; theoretically, it is derived from dependent origination and impermanence. Some scholars therefore stress that the Buddha's primary intention in teaching non-self was practical, and not a metaphysical assertion.

The tension between non-self and rebirth is the most central problem in Buddhist philosophy — see the two sections “The Ownership of Karma” and “Suffering in the Continuum” under this heading.

src.q: “Form is not self … all of it is to be observed as it really is as not self and not belonging to a self.” On hearing this, the five monks did not give rise to any taints, and their minds were liberated.
“Form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self; what is not self also does not belong to a self.”
The Pali counterpart, likewise spoken to the five monks.

tt.trans: Liu-Song dynasty, trans. Guṇabhadra, *Saṃyukta-āgama* (c. 435–443)

rel.nirvana: since there is no self there is no realiser; nirvāṇa is the cessation of suffering

name: The Provisional Self
desc:
The “self” posited in conformity with the conventions of the world: without substantial reality, yet functionally valid. Buddhism teaches [[anatta|non-self]] but does not deny the provisional self; within the [[conventional|conventional truth]] the provisional self holds, and it is the support of ethical responsibility, of the attribution of karmic fruit, and of speech and communication.

This is often misunderstood as a self-contradiction in Buddhism, but it is in fact a distinction of two levels: ultimately there is no substantially real self, while conventionally “self” is valid as a designated concept. Without the provisional self, “who acts, who receives the fruit, who practises” could not be stated at all, and both ethics and practice would lose their footing.

Among the schools, the Vātsīputrīyas held that there is an “inexpressible pudgala,” attempting to give a substantial answer between non-self and the attribution of karmic fruit, and were criticised by the other schools as “non-Buddhist teachers attached to the Buddha's Dharma.” This controversy shows precisely how delicate the status of the provisional self is: call it a mere designation, and the attribution of karmic fruit cannot be explained; call it substantially real, and non-self is contravened.

src.q: Throughout the sūtra, “I,” “sentient being” and the like are repeatedly used as provisional designations conforming to worldly convention.
Refutes the Vātsīputrīya claim that the pudgala is substantially real, and establishes the [[pudgala|provisional self]].

src.t: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-only), fascicle 1
src.q: Distinguishes the provisional self from the real self.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (usage as a conventional designation)
tt.fix: The Vātsīputrīya doctrine of the pudgala and its criticism in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, c. 2nd–5th century

name: Neither One Nor Different
desc:
The successive moments of a [[continuity|continuum]] are neither identical nor wholly unrelated; they are a “similar continuum.” This is the explanatory core that allows [[anatta|non-self]] and rebirth to coexist.

“Not one”: if earlier and later were entirely identical, there could be no change, no practice and no liberation; “not different”: if earlier and later were wholly unrelated, karmic fruit could not be attributed, and memory and responsibility would lose their basis. The “similar continuum” falls precisely between these two extremes.

This formulation was later expanded in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* into one pair of the “eight negations” (neither one nor different), and became the general formula by which Madhyamaka handles every question of identity: wherever earlier and later, self and other, or the universal and the particular are involved, they are explained by neither-one-nor-different.

src.q: “Neither one nor different” is one of the eight negations, setting forth the middle way by way of negation.

src.t: *Milindapañha* (Naxian Biqiu Jing, the Chinese version of the Questions of Milinda)
src.q: Uses the simile of the lamp and the simile of the chariot to explain that earlier and later are neither one nor different.

tt.form: c. 5th–2nd century BCE (the idea of the continuum)
tt.fix: “Neither one nor different” as a general Madhyamaka formula appears in the *Madhyamaka-kārikā* (c. 150–250)

name: The Ownership of Karma
desc:
The relation is not one of ownership but of causal connection: present [[ignorance|ignorance]], craving and grasping, and karmic force are constituting the suffering of the next life.

This is the most standard Buddhist way of answering “if there is [[anatta|non-self]], who receives the fruit?” — it shifts the question from “who” to “how.” “The ownership of karma” does not mean that some entity holds karma, but is the causal connection between karma and the suffering that follows.

Thus “the one who suffers in the next life” is neither “you” nor “someone else,” but: suffering in the continuum. Here “you” and “someone else” are both substantialising expressions, and what Buddhism sets out to show is precisely this: the relation of the continuum cannot be reduced to any kind of substantial attribution.

This answer still leaves room for philosophical discussion (the problem of identity), but it is at least not vague: it explicitly redefines “ownership” as “causal connection,” and thereby makes the doctrine of karmic fruit and the doctrine of non-self hold within one and the same framework.

src.t: *Milindapañha* (Naxian Biqiu Jing, the Chinese version of the Questions of Milinda)
src.q: Answers “if there is [[anatta|non-self]], who receives the fruit?” with the simile of the lamp and the simile of milk and curds.
The scholastic exposition of how karmic fruit continues in the [[continuity|continuum]] without being lost.
The argument that “agent and receiver” are not obtainable as either one or different.

tt.trans: *Milindapañha* (Chinese translation c. 3rd century, recording the questions of King Milinda)

name: Suffering in the Continuum
desc:
“The one who suffers in the next life” is not “you,” nor “someone else” — it is suffering in the continuum. Likewise, [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]] is not realised by a “who,” but is the cessation of suffering and the stilling of the [[continuity|continuum]].

This formulation joins the two endpoints of the doctrine of non-self into a single line: at the starting point there is no “I” wandering in saṃsāra, and at the endpoint there is no “I” entering nirvāṇa. Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are therefore both descriptions of the process that is the “continuum,” and not descriptions of some subject.

It also yields a practical corollary: since what suffers is the continuum and not a substance, “the cessation of suffering” need not be achieved by destroying or satisfying some self; it is enough to still the conditions of the continuum (ignorance, craving and grasping).

src.q: “When this does not exist, that does not exist; with the cessation of this, that ceases.” — the cessation of suffering is the stilling of the [[continuity|continuum]].

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: Since there is [[anatta|non-self]] there is no realiser; nirvāṇa is the cessation of suffering.
[[nirvana|Nirvāṇa]] is emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness.

name: Dependent origination
desc:
“When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.” All dharmas arise in dependence on conditions and cease in dependence on conditions; they possess no independent own-nature. This is the general principle of Buddhist causality and the point that distinguishes Buddhism from the other śramaṇa currents of its age: it rejects alike the Brahmanical “theory of divine determination,” in which Brahmā creates all things, and fatalism and accidentalism.

Both facets of the formula must be grasped together:
(1) arising / continuation — when the conditions that sustain suffering are present, the phenomena concerned arise or persist;
(2) cessation / reversion — when the conditions cease, the suffering that persisted in dependence on them ceases as well.

The passage comes from the [[doc_1|Saṃyukta-āgama (Za Ahan Jing)]], fascicle 10, sūtra 262: Kātyāyana asks “by what cause and by what condition is it called [[right_view|right view]],” and the Buddha answers, “One who sees the arising of the world as it really is does not give rise to the view of the non-existence of the world; one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is does not give rise to the view of the existence of the world. The Tathāgata, apart from the two extremes, teaches the middle way.” Dependent origination is therefore not merely a causal description; it is itself the “middle way” — precisely because one does not grasp at existence or at non-existence can one account for both continuation and reversion.

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicle 10, sūtra 262 (Taishō Tripiṭaka, vol. 2, p. 67a)
src.q: “It is said: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises — namely, with [[ignorance|ignorance]] as condition, formations, and so on up to the arising of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering. It is said: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases — namely, with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease, and so on up to the cessation of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering.”
Another occurrence of the same formula.
“Monks, with [[ignorance|ignorance]] as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.”
Another locus of detailed exposition in the Pali tradition.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the core content of the Buddha's awakening)
tt.fix: The formula fixed in *Saṃyukta-āgama* sūtras 262, 298, 335, and 358; parallel transmission in *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12 and *Dīgha Nikāya* 15
tt.trans: Translated into Chinese as the *Saṃyukta-āgama* by Guṇabhadra under the Liu Song dynasty (c. 435–443)

rel.karma: its unfolding at the ethical level

name: The twelve links
desc:
[[ignorance|Ignorance]] → formations → consciousness → [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]] → the six sense bases → contact → feeling → craving → clinging → becoming → birth → aging-and-death. The twelve links set out the complete cycle of the continuation of life.

The twelve links are not a linear time axis but a self-closing circle: after the final member, aging-and-death, ignorance begins again. They are described in two ways: forward observation (the gate of continuation) explains how saṃsāra takes shape, and reverse observation (the gate of reversion) states that “with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases … with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death cease.” One and the same chain, two directions.

“Forward and reverse observation” and “continuation and reversion” are not entirely synonymous: the former sometimes refers to the direction in which the twelve links are observed, the latter to the arising and the cessation of suffering.

The Tiantai school speaks in addition of “the twelve links in a single moment of thought” — the twelve links are complete within one moment of thought, without waiting for the crossing of three lives. This turns the twelve links from a temporal sequence of actual events into a present structure of mind-contemplation.

The twelve links are the most complete working-out of the Buddhist proposition that “causes and effects continue without any substantial self”: no member of the chain takes on the role of “who is reborn,” so that saṃsāra becomes a “process” rather than “the transfer of a substance.”

src.q: It opens with “when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises,” and then sets out the arising of the twelve links.
The fixed arrangement of the twelve links and the definition of each member.
Contains a particularly detailed exposition of the mutual relation between [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]] and consciousness.

tt.fix: The fixed formula of the twelve links appears in *Saṃyukta-āgama* fascicle 12 and *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12; “the twelve links in a single moment of thought” is a later development by the Tiantai school

name: Formations
desc:
The three karmas of body, speech, and mind as driven by [[ignorance|ignorance]], referring specifically to karma capable of bringing about future fruition. It is divided into meritorious formations (wholesome karma, which brings the pleasant fruits of the heavens and the human realm), non-meritorious formations (unwholesome karma, which brings the painful fruits of the three evil destinies), and imperturbable formations (the karma of meditative absorption, which brings the fruits of the form realm and the formless realm).

The placing of “formations” here is crucial: it shows that the starting point of the twelve links is not “a soul” but “the activity impelled by ignorance.” The motive force of saṃsāra is “activity” rather than “substance” from the very first member.

src.q: “With [[ignorance|ignorance]] as condition, formations.”
The threefold division into meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations.

tt.fix: The threefold division appears in the Sarvāstivāda treatises

name: Consciousness
desc:
Within the [[twelve_links|twelve links]] this refers specifically to the “rebirth consciousness,” the single moment of consciousness first conceived under the pull of past karma, not the faculty of discernment in general.

This member has been repeatedly reinterpreted in different systems: the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] explains it as the “linking consciousness”; the Yogācāra school unfolds it into eight consciousnesses and, by having the ālaya-vijñāna retain seeds and receive perfuming, makes “consciousness” carry at once the three functions of conception, seed-retention, and continuation, so that it becomes the crucial link in rebirth without a self. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Jie Shenmi Jing) says that the ālaya-vijñāna “follows along with the body and holds it fast,” which accords precisely with this member.

src.q: “With formations as condition, consciousness.”
The linking consciousness and the retention of seeds by the [[alaya|ālaya-vijñāna]].

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, “Chapter on the Marks of Mind, Manas, and Consciousness” (Xin Yi Shi Xiang Pin)
src.q: The scriptural source for the [[alaya|ālaya-vijñāna]] “holding fast to the body.”

tt.fix: The sense of “rebirth consciousness” appears in the school treatises; the system of eight consciousnesses was compiled by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu around the 4th–5th centuries

name: Name-and-form
desc:
“Name” refers to the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; “form” refers to the matter derived from the four great elements. Mentality and materiality combine to constitute the initial structure of individual life.

“Name-and-form” cannot be understood simply as “soul and body” — “name” (nāma) is a collection of four kinds of mental activity, and “form” (rūpa) is material existence; neither is a substance. In the *[[doc_21|Mahānidāna-sutta (Da Yinyuan Jing)]]* name-and-form and consciousness are said to depend on each other: consciousness dwells supported by name-and-form, and name-and-form grows nourished by consciousness, standing like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. This formulation of “mutual dependence” is precisely where the doctrine of [[anatta|non-self]] lands in the genesis of life.

src.q: “Consciousness dwells supported by [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]], and name-and-form grows nourished by consciousness … as two bundles of reeds stand by leaning against and supporting each other.”
“With consciousness as condition, [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]].”

tt.fix: The simile of the bundles of reeds leaning against each other appears in the *Mahānidāna-sutta* and in the corresponding Chinese translations

name: The six sense bases
desc:
The six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind gradually become complete and serve as the six gates for cognizing outer objects. Strictly speaking, the “six sense bases” (six āyatanas) are the entrances through which the six faculties face the six objects, not merely the six faculties themselves — “base” (āyatana) carries both the sense of inner bases (the six faculties) and outer bases (the six objects).

It is the intermediary between [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]] and “contact”: only when the six sense bases exist can the concurrence of faculty, object, and consciousness take place, and contact become contact with a content.

src.t: *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing), fascicles 12 and 8 (the section on the six sense bases)
src.q: “With [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]] as condition, the six sense bases.”

src.t: *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35 (the section on the six sense bases)
src.q: A systematic exposition of the six inner bases and the six outer bases.

tt.fix: The complete classification of the six sense bases / twelve bases appears in *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35 and in the Sarvāstivāda treatises

name: Contact
desc:
Contact arising from the concurrence of faculty, object, and consciousness. The treatises emphasize in particular that contact is not the coarse event of “the body touching an object” but the critical point at which cognition occurs — the fulfilment of the three conditions is called contact.

Contact is the immediate precondition of feeling and therefore also the first gate through which affliction arises. The scriptures often take “contact” as the watershed of all pleasurable and painful experience: if at contact one does not attend and does not give rise to grasping, then the craving and clinging that follow do not come about. This point of observation is the basis for the later practice of “guarding the gates of the six faculties.”

src.q: “With the [[link_sadayatana|six sense bases]] as condition, contact.”
The fixed formulation “contact is the concurrence of the three things.”

name: Feeling
desc:
The three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity, which are the immediate condition for the arising of craving. The scriptures distinguish three feelings (suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure), and the treatises further distinguish five feelings (adding grief and joy).

“Feeling” is neutral — feeling itself is not affliction, but an untrained mind inevitably reacts to feeling: to pleasant feeling it responds with greed, to painful feeling with aversion, to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling with delusion. The “contemplation of feeling” among the [[four_foundations|the four establishments of mindfulness]] begins precisely here: observing the arising and passing away of feeling as it really is, without reacting.

src.q: “With contact as condition, feeling.”
A detailed exposition of the contemplation of feeling — observing pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and whether they are defiled or undefiled.

tt.fix: The division into three feelings / five feelings appears in the treatises

name: Clinging

src.q: “With craving as condition, clinging.”
The fourfold division into clinging to sense desire, clinging to views, clinging to rules and vows, and clinging to the doctrine of self.

tt.fix: The four names of clinging appear in the school treatises

name: Becoming
desc:
Divided into becoming in the realm of desire, becoming in the form realm, and becoming in the formless realm; it refers specifically to the existence of karmic force capable of bringing about future fruition.

“Becoming” is the member that joins what precedes to what follows: viewed from cause, it is the accumulation of karmic force induced by clinging; viewed from result, it is the realm in which a new round of life is situated. The same member can therefore be explained either as “becoming as karma” (cause) or as “becoming as rebirth” (result) — the schools interpret this differently.

“Becoming” and “karma” coincide closely here, which shows that the tenth member of the [[twelve_links|twelve links]] and the doctrine of karmic force are different formulations of one and the same content.

src.q: “With clinging as condition, becoming.”
The threefold division into becoming in the realm of desire, the form realm, and the formless realm.

tt.fix: The classification of the three kinds of becoming appears in the treatises

name: Birth
desc: The assumption of a new round of life. The treatises define it as “the first linking of birth within the aggregates” — that is, the first moment of being conceived in a given destiny. “Birth” is therefore not the everyday word “being born” but a precise technical concept: the fresh beginning of [[continuity|continuity]].

src.q: “With becoming as condition, birth.”
“Birth” is said to mean “the first arising within the shared class of beings.”

name: Aging-and-death
desc: Decay and termination, together with the sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering that follow upon them. The treatises attach “sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair” to aging-and-death because aging-and-death is not itself the end — the emotional and psychological consequences it brings lie equally within the chain and lead directly to the next round of [[ignorance|ignorance]].

src.q: “With birth as condition, [[link_aging_death|aging-and-death]], sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.”

name: Three lives and two sets of cause and effect
aka: san shi liang chong yin guo
three lives two sets of causality
desc:
Past causes ([[ignorance|ignorance]], formations) → present results (consciousness, [[link_namarupa|name-and-form]], the six sense bases, contact, feeling); present causes (craving, clinging, becoming) → future results (birth, aging-and-death). The twelve links are thereby organized into two sets of causal relation.

This mode of organization turns the twelve links from the observation of “arising all at once in a single moment” into an interpretation “unfolded across lives,” which clarifies the causal structure of saṃsāra, but it also raises the question “what is it that continues from one life to the next” — precisely the core difficulty that later theories such as the ālaya-vijñāna and the doctrine of continuity were meant to address.

src.q: The twelve links are allotted according to “[[three_lives|three lives and two sets of cause and effect]]”: observed forward, saṃsāra is seen; observed in reverse, reversion is seen.
The various masters assign the stages of the twelve links differently.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the twelve links themselves)
tt.fix: The organization into “three lives and two sets of cause and effect” was fixed in the Sarvāstivāda treatises (c. 2nd–4th centuries)

name: Delusion, karma, and suffering
desc:
[[ignorance|Ignorance]] (delusion) → formations (karma) → consciousness through feeling (suffering) → craving and clinging (delusion) → becoming (karma) → birth and [[link_aging_death|aging-and-death]] (suffering). Affliction, action, and result condition one another, forming a self-perpetuating cycle.

The value of this threefold structure of “delusion, karma, suffering” is that it compresses the twelve links into three kinds of motive force and reveals that the cycle sustains itself because “suffering” in turn becomes the soil of the next round of “delusion” — feeling conditions craving and craving conditions clinging, so it is precisely suffering that gives rise to new affliction. The chain is therefore not a one-way causality but a closed loop with feedback.

src.q: The twelve links are subsumed under the three classes of delusion, karma, and event (suffering).
The three defilements of “delusion, karma, and suffering” are used to explain the [[continuity|continuity]] of what precedes and what follows.

tt.fix: The threefold division of delusion, karma, and suffering was fixed in the treatises

name: Forward and reverse observation
desc:
Forward observation is the gate of continuation, explaining how [[samsara|saṃsāra]] takes shape; reverse observation is the gate of reversion: “with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases … with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death cease.” One and the same chain, two directions.

This twofold direction shows what is distinctive about dependent origination: it is not a one-way law of causality but a system of conditions — when the conditions are complete, things arise; when they are not, things cease. “Liberation” therefore requires no additional transcendent cause; it requires only that the conditions be reversed. This is the structure of the Buddhist non-theistic soteriology.

src.q: The sūtra sets out together the two facets of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]], its arising and its cessation.
“With the cessation of [[ignorance|ignorance]], formations cease … thus the mass of suffering ceases.”

name: Karma

src.q: “With formations as condition, consciousness”; formations are karmic formations.

src.t: *Madhyama-āgama* (Zhong Ahan Jing), *Si Jing* (Sūtra on Volition), and others
src.q: Volition is taken as the substance of karma.
A systematic classification by kind, by realm-affiliation, and by the time of fruition.
It argues that karma is neither divine punishment, nor mechanical, nor fatalistic.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the basic claims of karma and causality)
tt.fix: The classifications of definite / indefinite, fruition in this / the next / a later life, and shared / individual appear in the Sarvāstivāda treatises (c. 2nd–4th centuries)

name: Ripening

src.q: The definition of the three senses of [[vipaka|ripening]] (ripening at a different time, of a different kind, and by transformation).
The [[vipaka|ripening]] consciousness is used to explain the retention of seeds and the reception of fruition.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the idea of karmic fruition)
tt.fix: The three senses of “ripening” (ripening at a different time, of a different kind, and by transformation) appear in the *Cheng Weishi Lun Shu Ji*, fascicle 2

name: Classifications of karma
desc:
Definite and indefinite karma; fruition in this life, in the next life, and in a later life; shared and individual karma. These three groups of classification answer three questions respectively: whether the fruition can be changed (definite / indefinite), when it is received (this life / the next / a later life), and by whom it is borne (shared / individual).

The existence of “indefinite karma” and of “fruition in a later life” is the technical guarantee that the Buddhist view of karmic fruition does not fall into mechanical determinism; the distinction between “shared karma” and “individual karma” serves to explain why the circumstances of the individual and the world in which that individual lives (age, environment, society) cannot each be accounted for independently.

src.q: The assignment of definite and indefinite karma, karma of the three times, and shared and individual karma.
“Karma is decisive,” “karma is predominant,” and so forth, are used to explain the relation between karma and its fruit.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the principle of karmic fruition)
tt.fix: The systematization of the three groups of classification appears in the Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra treatises

name: The three criteria for judging wholesomeness
desc:
(1) Judged by root: greed, aversion, and delusion are unwholesome; absence of greed, absence of aversion, and absence of delusion are wholesome. This is a judgment from the motive, whence they are also called the “three wholesome roots” and the “three unwholesome roots.”
(2) Judged by result: what leads to the suffering of self and others is unwholesome; what leads to the happiness of self and others is wholesome. “Happiness” here must be understood comprehensively — including the two levels of the present life and the ultimate, the two sides of self and others, and the two measures of the short term and the long term. An action that brings happiness in the short term but suffering in the long term, or happiness to one person but suffering to many, must still be judged unwholesome.
(3) Judged by the ultimate: what binds one to birth-and-death is wholesome with outflows; what leads to liberation and enlightenment is wholesome without outflows. This criterion gives “wholesome action” itself layers: if giving and observing precepts do not depart from grasping at self, they remain with outflows and can bring the fruits of the heavens and the human realm but cannot lead beyond.

The effect of applying the three criteria together is that Buddhist judgment of good and evil looks neither only at motive (otherwise atrocities could be justified by “good intentions”) nor only at result (otherwise one could not explain why wholesome action still binds), but judges motive, effect, and ultimate direction together. This too is the point of fundamental divergence between Buddhist ethics and the two extremes of “moral relativism” and “consequentialism.”

src.q: Absence of greed, absence of aversion, and absence of delusion are taken as the three wholesome roots.
The determination of wholesome mental factors and afflictive mental factors.
The distinction between wholesome with outflows and wholesome without outflows.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the three wholesome roots)
tt.fix: The layered organization of the three criteria appears in the treatises

name: Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate
desc:
Wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and the “indeterminate dharmas” that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. The [[three_natures|three natures]] (here the “three natures” mean wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, which share a name with but differ in meaning from the three natures of the imagined / dependent / perfected in [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]]) are the basic framework by which the treatises make value judgments about all dharmas.

The existence of the “indeterminate” is extremely important: it means that not all actions and mental states can be assigned to wholesome or unwholesome — breathing, walking, and unconscious gazing are all indeterminate. Were indeterminate dharmas forcibly drawn into the dichotomy of wholesome and unwholesome, ethical judgment would lose its discriminative power. The treatises therefore further distinguish the “obscured indeterminate” (covered by affliction yet in itself neither wholesome nor unwholesome, such as the innate self-grasping of the manas) from the “unobscured indeterminate.”

src.q: All dharmas are subsumed under the [[three_natures|three natures]] of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The distinction between the obscured indeterminate and the unobscured indeterminate.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the dichotomy of wholesome and unwholesome)
tt.fix: The three natures (wholesome / unwholesome / indeterminate) as a framework of subsumption in the treatises was fixed around the 2nd–4th centuries

name: The ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses of action
desc:
The ten unwholesome: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, greed, aversion, and wrong view. The ten wholesome are their opposites (not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not chattering idly, not being greedy, not being averse, and not holding wrong view).

“Wrong view” requires particular note: it does not refer generally to “erroneous opinions” but specifically to the view that denies causality and denies the four truths — that is, holding that there is no karmic fruition of good and evil, no this world and no next world, and no [[four_truths|Four Noble Truths]]. This is the only member of the ten unwholesome that belongs to “view,” and though it stands last, it is the ground on which the preceding nine are established: if there is no causality, then killing and stealing are not wrong either.

The ten wholesome and ten unwholesome are the most widely used classification in Buddhist ethics and the main content of the “[[folk_layer|folk layer]]” — vernacular religious forms such as tales of karmic retribution and hell-tableaux mostly take the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome as their narrative framework.

src.q: The enumeration of the ten wholesome courses of action and the ten unwholesome courses of action.

The definition, in the contemplation of dharmas, of the “ten unwholesome courses of action” and the “ten wholesome courses of action,” stating explicitly that wrong view means “no giving, no offering, no sacrifice, no [[vipaka|ripening]] of the fruits of good and evil action … no this world and no other world.”
A detailed exposition of the [[ten_paths|ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses of action]].

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the content of the ten wholesome and unwholesome courses)
tt.fix: The fixed enumeration appears in *Dīgha Nikāya* 22 and in the treatises
tt.trans: The popularization of the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome and the tales of retribution belong to the folk layer and flourished in China from the Tang and Song onward

name: Saṃsāra

src.q: “With [[ignorance|ignorance]] as condition, formations, and so on up to the arising of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering.” — Saṃsāra is the arising of the mass of suffering.
The teaching of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] as an account of the structure of saṃsāra.
The sense of continuation, of flowing on.

tt.fix: The philosophical exposition of the sense of “continuity” appears in the school treatises and the Mahāyāna śāstras

rel.continuity: that is, continuity, not the relocation of a substance

name: The six realms
desc:
Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell beings. These describe the different states of existence brought about by karma.

One must note a difference among the schools: the sectarian schools of early Buddhism mostly speak of “five destinies” (nivāsa), that is, without the asuras — asuras are assigned to the destiny of ghosts or to that of the gods; the Mahāyāna mostly speaks of “six realms,” making the asuras a separate destiny. This difference is often mistaken for a doctrinal disagreement, whereas in fact it is mainly a difference in classificatory habit.

Another point for understanding: the six realms are not six geographical places but primarily “states of existence brought about by karma.” The treatises accordingly also say that “a single mind comprises the ten dharma-realms” (Tiantai) — the six realms together with the four noble realms make ten realms, all of which appear in accordance with a single present moment of thought. This reading turns the six realms from cosmology into a theory of mind-nature.

src.q: A systematic exposition of the [[six_realms|six realms]].
The assignment of the five destinies (the asuras are not a separate destiny).
The scriptural basis for the ten dharma-realms.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the doctrine of five destinies)
tt.fix: The schools mostly speak of five destinies and the Mahāyāna mostly of six realms; the organization of the ten dharma-realms belongs to the Tiantai school (6th century)
tt.trans: The popularization of hell-tableaux and of the details of the six realms belongs to the folk layer

name: Continuity
desc:
The continuity of the consciousness aggregate, the continuity of karmic force, the continuity of craving, and the continuity of the [[five_aggregates|five aggregates]]. [[samsara|Saṃsāra]] is continuity, not the relocation of a substance.

“Continuity” (santāna) is the central concept by which Buddhism deals with the problem of identity: successive moments are not the same (otherwise there would be permanence without need of effort), nor are they unrelated (otherwise karmic fruition could not be attributed), but are a “similar continuity.” This formulation replaces “substantial identity” with “causal relatedness,” and “substratum” with “flow.”

The Yogācāra school explains how continuity is possible by the retention of seeds in the ālaya-vijñāna; the Madhyamaka says that continuity is like an illusion and “falls into neither annihilation nor permanence”; the two address different levels of the same difficulty.

src.q: “With the cessation of this, that ceases” — the conditional account of [[continuity|continuity]].
The [[alaya|ālaya-vijñāna]] “constantly turns like a violent stream,” explaining continuity.
The emptiness of own-nature of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] is used to explain continuity that falls into neither annihilation nor permanence.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the idea of continuity)
tt.fix: The Yogācāra theory of continuity through seed-retention dates from c. the 4th–5th centuries; the Madhyamaka theory of continuity as illusion from c. the 2nd–3rd centuries

name: The lamp-transmission analogy
desc:
As a flame passing to a lamp, lamp continuing from lamp in [[continuity|continuity]] — not the same fire, yet not unrelated. This is the simile most often used to understand “[[anatta|non-self]] yet rebirth.”

The key to the simile lies in two places: first, “fire” is not a permanently existing substance but only the continuity of a process of combustion; second, the later fire arises from the earlier fire, so that there is connection without identity. There are also passages in the scriptures that use “firewood” as a condition to explain that fire is neither permanent nor annihilated. The simile is also used to answer the challenge “if there is no self, who receives the fruit?”: what receives the fruit is not some entity but this very process of continuity.

src.q: A lamp and a fire are used to explain [[continuity|continuity]] and unreality.

src.t: *Milindapañha* (Naxian Biqiu Jing, the Chinese version of the Questions of Milinda)
src.q: The lamp simile is used to answer “if there is [[anatta|no-self]], who receives the fruit?”
Similes such as “a lamp does not illuminate itself” are used to explain that one falls into neither existence nor non-existence.

tt.trans: The *Milindapañha* (Chinese translation c. 3rd century) uses this simile to answer Greek-style questioning

name: Dharma

src.q: The polysemous uses of “dharma” occur throughout the sūtras.
It defines dharma as “that which is able to hold its own characteristic,” and posits the [[five_paths|five categories]] and seventy-five dharmas.
The classificatory system of the [[five_paths|five categories]] and one hundred dharmas.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the usages as teaching and as phenomenon)
tt.fix: The sense of “dharma-substance” and the fivefold classification appear in the Sarvāstivāda treatises (c. 2nd–4th centuries); the five categories and one hundred dharmas appear in the Yogācāra treatises

name: Conditioned dharmas
desc:
Arising from the confluence of causes and conditions, fashioned, arising and ceasing, impermanent. It covers the four classes of [[rupa|material dharmas]], mental dharmas, [[caitasika|mental factors]], and dharmas dissociated from mind.

The literal sense of “conditioned” (saṃskṛta) is “made by fashioning.” The mark of a conditioned dharma is therefore the four characteristics: arising, duration, change, and cessation — whatever has the mark of arising and ceasing belongs to the conditioned. The Sarvāstivāda holds that the four characteristics are real dharmas, whereas the Sautrāntika and the Yogācāra hold that they are posited stages.

All conditioned dharmas are impermanent and therefore also suffering (the suffering of formations) — “because it is impermanent, it is suffering” is an inference that recurs throughout the Āgamas.

src.q: “All formations are impermanent” and the definition of [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]].
The fourfold classification into [[rupa|material dharmas]], mental dharmas, mental factors, and dharmas dissociated from mind.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the sense of impermanence)
tt.fix: The fourfold classification and the debate over the reality or the positedness of the four characteristics appear in the school treatises

name: Unconditioned dharmas

src.q: It posits analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, and space as the [[three_unconditioned|three unconditioned dharmas]] and asserts that unconditioned dharmas are really existent.
It posits the six unconditioned dharmas: space, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, imperturbability, the cessation of perception and feeling, and [[suchness|suchness]].
Through the emptiness of own-nature of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] it explains the non-duality of the conditioned and the unconditioned.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (nirvāṇa as the unfashioned)
