tt.fix: The three unconditioned dharmas (Sarvāstivāda, c. 2nd–4th centuries); the six unconditioned dharmas (Yogācāra, c. 5th–7th centuries)

name: The five aggregates

src.q: “Form is not the self. If form were the self, no affliction or suffering would arise in regard to form, and one could not have one's wish in regard to form: ‘Let it be thus, let it not be thus.’ … All that is to be observed, as it really is, as neither self nor belonging to a self.” — The counterpart of the Pali *[[anatta|Anattalakkhaṇa-sutta]]*; on hearing this the five monks attained arhatship.
“Form is impermanent; the impermanent is suffering; the suffering is not self; what is not self is also not what belongs to a self. To contemplate thus is called true and correct observation.”
The Pali counterpart, likewise spoken to the five monks.

tt.trans: Translated into Chinese as the *Saṃyukta-āgama* by Guṇabhadra under the Liu Song dynasty; Yijing of the Tang also translated the *Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates*, which may be consulted in addition

name: Material dharmas
desc:
Material existence — the four great elements (earth, water, fire, and wind) and the matter derived from them — belonging to the [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]]; that is, the form aggregate among the five aggregates.

The original sense of “form” (rūpa) is related to “deterioration and resistance”: what deteriorates and offers resistance is called form. The treatises divide material dharmas into eleven: the five faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body), the five objects (visible form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects), and unmanifest form (or form included in the dharma base). Modern readers often mistakenly take “form” to mean colour, whereas it is the whole category of the material.

src.q: The elevenfold classification of [[rupa|material dharmas]] and the definition by “deterioration and resistance.”
“All form, whether past, future, or present … all that is not self.”

tt.fix: The elevenfold classification of material dharmas appears in the Sarvāstivāda treatises

name: Mental factors
desc:
Mental activities that arise together with the mind as sovereign, such as feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, greed, aversion, and delusion. “Mental factors” arise in association with the “mind as sovereign” and are the concrete content of “mind.”

The grouping of mental factors in the treatises best reveals the differences among the schools' systems: the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] posits forty-six mental factors (in six groups: universal dharmas, dharmas universally wholesome, dharmas universally afflictive, dharmas universally unwholesome, dharmas of minor affliction, and indeterminate dharmas); the [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]] posits fifty-one mental factors (in six groups: universal, particular, wholesome, root afflictions, secondary afflictions, and indeterminate).

The system of mental factors is the most finely detailed part of Buddhist psychology — it breaks “affliction” down into identifiable and counterable items, giving practice a clear unit of operation.

src.q: The sixfold grouping of the forty-six mental factors.
The sixfold grouping of the fifty-one mental factors.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (basic mental factors such as feeling, perception, and volition)
tt.fix: Systematization of mental factors: forty-six in the Sarvāstivāda (c. 2nd–4th centuries); fifty-one in the Yogācāra (c. 5th–7th centuries)

name: The three unconditioned dharmas

src.q: “[[unconditioned|Unconditioned dharmas]] are of three kinds: first, analytical cessation; second, non-analytical cessation; third, space.”
A detailed debate concerning the [[three_unconditioned|three unconditioned dharmas]].

tt.form: c. 3rd–5th century CE (Sarvāstivādin scholastic doctrine) (nirvāṇa as non-analytical cessation)
tt.fix: The systematization of the three unconditioned dharmas and the claim of their real existence appear in the Sarvāstivāda treatises (c. 2nd–4th centuries)

name: The six unconditioned dharmas
desc:
Posited by the [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]]: space, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, imperturbability, the cessation of perception and feeling, and [[suchness|suchness]]. Suchness is taken as the perfected nature.

Compared with the three unconditioned dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda, the Yogācāra adds three: the unconditioned of imperturbability (attained by extinguishing the feelings of suffering and pleasure from the fourth dhyāna upward), the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling (attained in the attainment of cessation), and the unconditioned of suchness (revealed by the twofold emptiness of all dharmas).

The crucial point is that the Yogācāra includes “suchness” among the unconditioned and takes it as the perfected nature, thereby shifting the centre of gravity of unconditioned dharmas from “cessation” to “suchness” — that is, from “the cessation of what” to “what is manifesting as it really is.” This shift is the watershed between the Yogācāra and the Sarvāstivāda on the question of unconditioned dharmas.

src.q: The six unconditioned dharmas: space, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, imperturbability, the cessation of perception and feeling, and [[suchness|suchness]].
The place of the [[six_unconditioned|six unconditioned dharmas]] within the classification of dharmas dissociated from mind and unconditioned dharmas.

tt.form: c. 5th century (the line of Vasubandhu and Asaṅga)
tt.fix: The six unconditioned dharmas were fixed in the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (translated in 659)

name: Suchness

src.q: The “teaching of the seven kinds of [[suchness|suchness]]” — suchness becomes the ground of both continuation and reversion.
[[suchness|Suchness]] is taken as the perfected nature, “revealed by the twofold emptiness.”
“[[suchness|Suchness]] within affliction is called the tathāgatagarbha; suchness released from affliction is called the dharmakāya.”

src.t: *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Da Cheng Qixin Lun)
src.q: “One mind” is taken as “the great totality of the one dharma-realm,” opening the teaching of [[suchness|suchness]] as dependent origination.

tt.form: c. 5th century BCE (the sense of the real condition of dharmas)
tt.fix: The Yogācāra takes suchness as the perfected nature (4th–5th centuries); the “seven kinds of suchness” appear in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; the teaching of suchness as dependent origination appears in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (c. 6th century, a Chinese composition)

rel.tathagatagarbha: suchness released from affliction is the tathāgatagarbha

name: The three realms and the twenty-eight heavens
aka: san jie er shi ba tian
desire realm form realm formless realm

src.t: *Dīgha Nikāya* 1, *Brahmajāla-sutta* (Fanwang Jing); *Dīgha Nikāya* 2, *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (Shamen Guo Jing)
src.q: The enumeration of the [[three_realms|three realms]] and the various heavens, and the relation between the four dhyānas and the places of fruition.
The systematic exposition of the [[three_realms|three realms and twenty-eight heavens]] and the calculation of lifespans.

src.t: *Visuddhimagga* (Qingjing Daolun), “The Exposition of the Brahmā Abidings,” and others
src.q: The heavens and the fruition of the brahmā abidings in the [[southern_tradition|Southern tradition]].

tt.form: c. 5th–3rd centuries BCE (the beginnings of the doctrine of the three realms)
tt.fix: The systematic exposition of the twenty-eight heavens appears in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* fascicle 8 (4th–5th centuries) and in the Southern treatises (5th century)

rel.six_realms: the six realms and the three realms as two classifications

name: Kalpas and the phases of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness
aka: three thousand great thousand world system
desc:
The Buddhist scales of time and the extent of the cosmos, the precondition for understanding the claim that “[[samsara|saṃsāra]] is without beginning.”

**Kalpa** Traditionally its length is explained by a simile: as with a stone mountain forty li across, brushed once every hundred years with a soft fine cloth — when it is worn away, one kalpa has still not come to an end. Kalpas are divided into small, intermediate, and great kalpas, and one great kalpa comprises the four intermediate kalpas of **formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness** — the world passes through the four periods of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness, going round and round without beginning or end.

**The three thousand great thousand world system** With Mount Sumeru at the centre, the region illuminated by one sun and moon is one world (one small world); a thousand small worlds make a small thousand world, a thousand small thousand worlds make an intermediate thousand world, and a thousand intermediate thousand worlds make a great thousand world — together called the “three thousand great thousand world system,” the field of conversion of one Buddha. The Sahā world is the field of conversion of Śākyamuni Buddha, while the [[pure_land|land of bliss]] is the field of conversion of Amitābha Buddha.

**What this layer is meant to solve** Without these scales of time and space, “saṃsāra” and “sentient beings without bound” would be mere phrases: the number of sentient beings and the length of saṃsāra must exceed any imaginable scale for the bodhisattva path's “liberating all sentient beings” not to be a finite project. And it is precisely because worlds undergo formation and destruction and Buddhas appear and enter nirvāṇa that there is the question of the “continuity of the Buddha-seed” — this is the temporal background of the tathāgatagarbha teaching and the bodhisattva path.

src.t: *Dīgha Nikāya* 26, *Cakkavattisīhanāda-sutta* (Zhuanlun Shengwang Shizihou Jing), and others
src.q: The simile of the kalpa and the exposition of [[kalpa_cosmology|formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness]].

src.t: *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicles 11 and 12, “Exposition of the World”
src.q: The structure of the [[kalpa_cosmology|three thousand great thousand world system]] and the calculation of the great kalpa.
Chinese cosmological sūtras, which agree and differ in various respects with what the *[[doc_27|Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya (Jushe lun)]]* sets out.

tt.fix: The systematic calculation of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness and of the three thousand great thousand world system appears in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* fascicles 11–12 (4th–5th centuries)

rel.mahayana_origins: the background of many kalpas, many Buddhas, and the Buddhas of the ten directions

name: The Three Councils
desc:
The collective recitation and authorisation of the Buddha's teaching by his disciples after his parinirvāṇa. The original sense of “council” (saṃgīti) is “reciting together”: the participants recited the teaching in common and confirmed one another's recitation, rather than one person editing it. This is the starting point of the twofold structure of Dharma and Vinaya: Ānanda recited the Dharma (the sūtras) and Upāli recited the Vinaya.

Later tradition transmits chiefly three councils:

- **The first**: shortly after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, at Rājagṛha, with five hundred monks taking part and Kāśyapa presiding; Ānanda recited the sūtras and Upāli the Vinaya. The accounts given by [[southern_tradition|the Theravāda]] and by [[sarvastivada|the Sarvāstivāda]] agree on this in essentials.
- **The second**: a hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, at Vaiśālī, occasioned by the question whether the “ten points” of the Vṛjiputra monks were legitimate; seven hundred monks took part, and the ten points were judged illegitimate. The significance of this council lies not in its verdict but in the fact that **the division of the schools emerges here**: differing attitudes towards this council became the point of divergence between the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṃghikas.
- **The third**: here the accounts diverge most. The Theravāda (*Dīpavaṃsa*, *Mahāvaṃsa*) places it in the reign of Aśoka, presided over by Moggaliputtatissa, and has the Abhidharma-piṭaka compiled at it; the Sarvāstivāda places it in the reign of Kaniṣka, presided over by Pārśva and Vasumitra, and has the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā* compiled at it. The two accounts do not correspond to one and the same event but are each tradition's retrospective account of when the Abhidharma-piṭaka took shape.

Three points require attention. First, the accounts of the councils are themselves retrospective narratives of a later age, and the later the legend the more detailed it becomes; modern scholarship is reserved about their historicity. Second, Chinese translations preserve other lineages as well, such as the *Fu Fazang Yinyuan Zhuan* and the *Aśokāvadāna*, which do not agree with the Pali tradition. Third, the Mahāyāna has its own claim that Mañjuśrī and Maitreya compiled the Mahāyāna teachings, an independent narrative of another order that cannot be reconciled with the Theravāda tripiṭaka lineage.

name: Sarvāstivāda
desc:
The school among the nikāyas with the most systematic philosophy. It holds that “the three times are real and the substance of the dharmas is eternal”: the substance of dharmas past, present, and future is all real, and only their function arises, has not yet arisen, or has ceased, according to time.

This claim is not an arbitrary metaphysical preference but a way of accommodating the fruit of karma: if there were no substance of dharmas in past and future, on what ground would “karma already performed” ripen in a later life? The Sarvāstivāda therefore needs a substance of dharmas that does not vanish when its function ceases. This also explains why it posits at the same time “unmanifest form” (avijñapti-rūpa): a kind of [[rupa|form]] produced by bodily and verbal karma that is invisible and persists, and that serves to carry on [[jie_ti|the essence of the precepts]] and the continuity of karma.

The doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda (usually taken in the arrangement of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*): the five categories and seventy-five dharmas (eleven forms, one mind, forty-six mental factors, fourteen dharmas not associated with mind, and three unconditioned dharmas); the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths; the forty-six mental factors; and the coexistence of the reality of the three times with “perishing in every instant” (the substance of the dharmas is eternal while their function perishes in every instant — the two do not contradict each other).

Historically it was the dominant school of north-western India (Kaśmīra, Gandhāra), and it is at once the direct opponent and the source of Chinese Abhidharma and of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. Chinese scholars often come to know the Sarvāstivāda through the *Kośa*, but the school's own fuller position must be sought in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā*: the two differ on many details and must not be conflated.

name: Sautrāntika
desc:
The school that takes the sūtras as its norm and does not acknowledge the authority of [[abhidharma|the Abhidharma-piṭaka]]; “Sautrāntika” means “those whose measure is the sūtras.” “Measure” (pramāṇa) here means the criterion: what counts as a trustworthy source for the teaching. The Sautrāntika are therefore often called **the earliest critical school within Buddhism** — whatever the treatises say but the sūtras do not is not necessarily accepted.

Its core positions:

- **No substance in past and future** — the past and the future have no reality; only the present is real. This is a direct negation of the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] doctrine of “the reality of the three times”;
- **Continuity of seeds** — the preservation of karma does not depend on a real “unmanifest form” but on the functional distinction of “seeds” (bīja) and perfuming (vāsanā) upon the continuity of mind;
- **An epistemology of consciousness** — knowledge arises from the conjunction of object and consciousness; the object is what is cognised, and the way it is established became the starting point of later disputes between Yogācāra and pramāṇa theory.

Strictly speaking the Sautrāntika was not an organised school standing alongside the Sarvāstivāda so much as **a body of critical positions and methods** (its early representatives were mostly called “dārṣṭāntikas,” exponents of examples). Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* undertakes a general review of the Sarvāstivāda from this school's standpoint, and the *Kośa* is therefore often described as “refuting the Vaibhāṣikas by the meaning of the Sautrāntika.”

Its most important contribution to later thought is the concept of the “seed”: the Yogācāra doctrine that the ālaya-consciousness holds the seeds is precisely a systematisation of the Sautrāntika account of the continuity of seeds, developed from “a functional distinction upon the continuity of mind” into “the eighth consciousness containing the seeds.”

name: Consciousness Exists, the Object Does Not
desc:
The core thesis of Yogācāra: **the external object is not apart from consciousness** — the object cognised cannot be established independently of the cognising mind, and so it is said that “consciousness exists, the object does not.”

This thesis is often misread as “nothing exists at all.” Its actual meaning is that the very dichotomy of “object” and “consciousness” calls for examination: the object of which we are aware is always the object as presented by consciousness (the apprehended aspect), and an “object apart from consciousness” has never been given. This is therefore not a denial of phenomena but a denial of the assumption that “behind the phenomenon there is an existence independent of cognition.”

The mode of argument (the most frequently cited group among the arguments of the masters collected in the *[[doc_29|Cheng Weishi Lun]]*, the *Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-only*):

- the same object is seen differently by different beings (a hungry ghost sees water as pus and blood, a human sees it as water), from which it follows that the object is not independent;
- in dreams and in the perceptions of one with defective eyesight there is no external object, yet reactions of pleasure and pain still occur, from which it follows that “consciousness” can arise without an external object;
- if the object existed really apart from consciousness, it would have to be permanent and not depend on conditions, which contradicts experience.

Yogācāra places this thesis by means of the **[[three_natures|three natures]]**: the imagined nature (the own-nature of the object) is nonexistent, the dependent nature (the continuity of consciousness) exists, and the perfected nature (suchness made manifest by the two emptinesses) is real. “Consciousness exists, the object does not” is thus a single sentence compressing “the dependent nature exists while the imagined nature does not” — and confining “emptiness” to the imagined nature is precisely the crux of the divergence between Madhyamaka and Yogācāra.

name: Nāgārjuna
desc:
The founder of [[madhyamaka|the Madhyamaka school]], traditionally placed in the 2nd–3rd century (his dates cannot be fixed with certainty; the traditional biographies are largely marvellous and of limited value as historical sources). His writings were collected differently in the two systems of Chinese and Tibetan transmission:

- **Chinese transmission** — the “four treatises”: the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]*, the *Śataśāstra* (attributed to Āryadeva), the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The first three are those on which the Sanlun school relies; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is a commentary on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, vast in scale and containing Abhidharma-style extended analysis as well.
- **Tibetan transmission** — further works including the commentaries on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*, the *Śūnyatāsaptati*, the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, and the *Ratnāvalī*; the Tibetan tradition takes the commentarial lineage of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka, Candrakīrti) as its doctrinal criterion.

Nāgārjuna's contribution lies not in advancing new theses but in a **self-awareness of method**: “dependent origination is the absence of own-nature” — whatever arises from causes and conditions must lack an independent own-nature; lacking own-nature, the eight basic determinations of existence — arising, ceasing, permanence, annihilation, identity, difference, coming, going — are all untenable. This is the “middle way of the eight negations.”

The characteristic of his argument is that he refutes his opponent's self-contradictory thesis by **reductio ad absurdum** (prasaṅga) without himself establishing a thesis — hence Madhyamaka is often described as “refuting without establishing.” This method was later judged by the Chinese Sanlun school to be “refuting the false and revealing the true,” while in Tibet it gave rise to the division between the Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika.

Chinese reception of Nāgārjuna was indirect: his teaching was first translated by Kumārajīva (401–409) and then, through Sengquan and Falang, became a school under Jizang; its Chinese aspect therefore bears a strongly “refuting” colour, while the expansive side represented by the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* was comparatively little inherited.

src.q: “Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going.”

name: Madhyamaka
desc:
One of the two great tracks of Indian Mahāyāna, taking [[nagarjuna|Nāgārjuna]]'s *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* as its root and holding that “dependent origination is emptiness of own-nature, and emptiness of own-nature is dependent origination” — emptiness is not nothingness but “the absence of own-nature”; precisely because there is no own-nature, dependent origination holds.

The core group of theses:

- **Dependent origination, emptiness, provisional designation, and the middle way are one** — the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: “Whatever arises from causes and conditions, I say to be emptiness; that is also a provisional designation, and that is the meaning of the middle way.”
- **The two truths**: without relying on the conventional truth, the ultimate meaning is not attained; having attained the ultimate meaning, the conventional truth is not destroyed either. Emptiness therefore does not destroy causality or ethics.
- **No own-nature means no arising**: if a dharma had own-nature, it would not depend on conditions; since it does depend on conditions, it has no own-nature; having no own-nature, “arising” cannot be established as real.

Within India the school is distinguished into Bhāviveka (Svātantrika, holding that one may establish an argument independently by inference) and Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti (Prāsaṅgika, refuting others only by reductio). The Chinese transmission is carried by the Sanlun school; the Tibetan transmission takes Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka as its highest doctrine. The place of the same source in the two systems is very different: **the Chinese tradition treats it as one school among others, the “Sanlun school,” while the Tibetan tradition treats it as “the criterion of all doctrine.”**

A common misunderstanding is that “Madhyamaka equals nihilism.” The school's own self-definition is precisely the opposite: it is the middle way that “falls into neither extreme” — neither into “existence” (existence by own-nature) nor into “nonexistence” (annihilation). To say “everything is nonexistent” is likewise a positing of “own-nature,” and must equally be refuted.

name: Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika
desc:
A distinction within [[madhyamaka|the Madhyamaka school]] concerning **the method of argument**, formed in the 6th–7th century, and of far greater importance than a mere “dispute over method.”

**Buddhapālita — the Prāsaṅgika**: he refutes others only by reductio and establishes no thesis of his own. The reason is that if one set up a formal argument (thesis, reason, example), the “reason” one establishes would itself need own-nature in order to hold, whereas Madhyamaka refutes own-nature precisely; hence establishing anything of one's own is already self-contradictory.

**Bhāviveka — the Svātantrika**: he holds that one may use an “autonomous reason” — acknowledging at the conventional level that reason and example hold, and demonstrating emptiness by inference; otherwise one cannot debate with outsiders, nor can anyone enter emptiness through inference.

**Candrakīrti’s *Madhyamakāvatāra* (Ru [[doc_30|Zhong lun]])** and *Prasannapadā* take Buddhapālita's side and criticise Bhāviveka systematically, and the Prāsaṅgika thereby became the mainstream of Indian Madhyamaka.

**Its weight after transmission to Tibet**: the Tibetan tradition takes Prāsaṅgika as its highest doctrine, and the “vipaśyanā” chapter of Tsongkhapa's *Lamrim Chenmo* takes the Prāsaṅgika view as its criterion.

**The Chinese transmission has no such distinction**: Jizang's Sanlun school has no direct lineage relation to the interpretations of Bhāviveka and Candrakīrti. This is not because the Chinese transmission is “not true Madhyamaka,” but because two lines of transmission each developed a different interpretive system — and in reading Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism this is the point most easily mistaken for a question of who is “more orthodox.” The actual shape of Indian Madhyamaka must be based chiefly on the Tibetan translations and the Sanskrit manuscripts; the Chinese translations offer only one aspect of it.

name: Buddhist Logic (Hetuvidyā)
desc:
The Buddhist science of argument and of knowledge; the Sanskrit “hetuvidyā” means “the science of reasons” — the enquiry into what sort of reason (hetu) can make an argument hold.

**From five members to three** Early Buddhist logic, influenced by the Nyāya school, used the “five-member formulation” (thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion). Dignāga (c. 480–540) reduced it to **three members**: the thesis (the proposition to be established), the reason (the ground), and the example (the illustration). For instance: sound is impermanent (thesis); because it is produced (reason); whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a pot (example).

**The triple mark of the reason** A reason must satisfy three conditions in order to hold: it must be a property of the subject (the reason genuinely belongs to the object under discussion); it must be present in similar instances (it occurs in cases of the same kind); and it must be absent from dissimilar instances (it does not occur in counter-cases). This is the criterion for judging the validity of an argument, and the core of the Buddhist treatment of “logical necessity.”

**Direct perception and inference** Dignāga's *Pramāṇasamuccaya* establishes “two means of knowledge”: direct perception is awareness free of conceptual construction; inference is the cognition arrived at from a reason. **The distinctive feature of Buddhist pramāṇa theory is that it links epistemology to soteriology** — “knowing things as they are” is precisely [[right_view|right view]], and therefore “what counts as reliable cognition” is not a purely theoretical question.

**Dharmakīrti (c. 7th century)**, in the *Pramāṇavārttika* and the other six of his seven treatises on pramāṇa, argued further for the reliability of the means of knowledge, and these became the main curriculum of monastic education in Tibetan Buddhism. In the Chinese transmission, by contrast, hetuvidyā was brought in by Xuanzang and served mainly as **a tool of debate** rather than an independent discipline, an auxiliary to the doctrine of the Faxiang school: the *Nyāyapraveśa* and Kuiji's *Yinming Dashu*, are the principal Chinese texts of hetuvidyā.

One historical fact worth noting: **hetuvidyā declined in the Chinese transmission but became a prominent discipline in the Tibetan**. The Tibetan tradition combined pramāṇa theory with [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] (“Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka plus pramāṇa”) and developed an extremely rigorous education in debate, whereas the Chinese tradition consistently gave priority to “engaging in practice in reliance on the teaching.” This is one of the clearest divisions of methodological preference between the two Buddhist traditions.

name: Dispute: If There Is No Self, Who Receives the Fruit?
aka: who receives the fruit of karma
desc:
**The question** If there is [[anatta|non-self]], who is it that acts and who is it that receives the fruit? And how does karma pass from this life to the next?

**Position A: the Vātsīputrīya** — they posit an “inexpressible pudgala”: it is neither [[five_aggregates|the five aggregates]] nor apart from the five aggregates, and so it cannot be said to be “identical with the aggregates” or “apart from the aggregates”; it is real, and precisely for that reason “who acts, who receives the fruit, who is liberated” can be established.

**Position B: the Sarvāstivāda** — the pudgala is only a provisional designation; what is real is the five aggregates together with the continuity of karma comprised in “unmanifest form.” The Vātsīputrīya position is censured as “a heterodox sect attached to the Buddha's Dharma”: once a real existent is admitted, it contradicts “all dharmas are without self.”

**Position C: the Sautrāntika** — no entity is needed at all; the “continuity of seeds” suffices to explain the transmission of karma: karma is a functional distinction upon the continuity of mind.

**Position D: Yogācāra** — the ālaya-consciousness “holds the seeds and receives the perfuming,” forever turning like a torrent, neither permanent nor annihilated, and takes on this function.

**Position E: Madhyamaka** — the question itself can be dismantled: only if the “self” were an entity would “who receives the fruit” be meaningful; precisely because there is no entity, “receiving the fruit” is possible. Between karma and its fruit there is a relation of dependent origination, not one of ownership.

**The consensus within Buddhism** lies in the shift of the question: “who” (the ascription of an entity) is replaced by “how” (the causal connection). The schools differ over **how thick an assumption of entity this “how” requires** — from provisional designation to seeds to the eighth consciousness, the thickness increases.

src.q: The Vātsīputrīya positing of the “pudgala” and the controversy with the other schools.

name: Dispute: The Atom and the Partless Particle
aka: ji wei yu wu fang fen
desc:
**The question** Does the smallest unit of matter, the “atom” (paramāṇu), exist? And if it does, does it have parts (spatial divisions)?

**Position A: [[sarvastivada|the Sarvāstivāda]]** — the atom is real and is the smallest unit of [[rupa|form]]. To answer the objection that “an atom must have spatial parts and so can be divided further,” the Sarvāstivāda holds that the “partless atom” occupies no spatial part and therefore cannot be divided further; only the aggregation of many partless atoms produces form that has resistance.

**Position B: the Sautrāntika and Yogācāra** — they refute this: if the atom is partless, it cannot combine into a body with volume (things without parts, added to one another, still cannot constitute something that has parts); and if the atom has parts, it can be divided further, so the claim that it is real cannot hold. Yogācāra turns from this towards “no external object; it is only what consciousness manifests.”

**Position C: Madhyamaka** — the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*'s “Examination of the Six Faculties” and “Examination of the Three Characteristics,” among others, refutes the independence of the atom by the mutual dependence of “one and many” and of “part and whole”: if the atom is established in dependence on an “aggregate,” it cannot exist by own-nature; and if it existed by own-nature, it could not stand in dependence on an “aggregate.”

**Position D: the Vaiśeṣika school (a non-Buddhist school)** — it posits atoms as real; its position resembles the Sarvāstivādin claim in form but its system is different, and both sides refute the position that “the atom is empty.”

**The value of this dispute**: it is a rare philosophical debate within Buddhism conducted around **objects of physics and mathematics**. Although its conclusion tends towards “the atom is not real,” its mode of argument became the standard model for the Buddhist argument for “the absence of own-nature” (refuting own-nature by the mutual dependence of “part” and “what has parts”).

name: Dispute: The Two Truths as Reality or as Teaching
aka: er di de ti yu jiao
desc:
**The question** Are the “[[two_truths|two truths]]” two kinds of **reality** (objects), or two kinds of **statement** (teaching)?

**Position A: [[sarvastivada|the Sarvāstivāda]]** — the two truths are two kinds of object: the ultimate truth is constituted by real dharmas that “exist by own-nature,” the conventional truth by aggregates that “exist as provisional designation.” Both truths are therefore “truths” (realities); they differ only in level.

**Position B: Madhyamaka (the Sanlun school)** — it principally holds the “**two truths as verbal teaching**”: the two truths are two forms of the Buddha's preaching, not a principle to be realised or an object to be contemplated. The two truths are therefore not two worlds but two ways of formulating one and the same reality; if the two truths were taken as two kinds of object, they would become “two entities,” which contradicts “non-duality.”

**Position C: the Tiantai school** — “the two truths open out into three truths, and the three truths are the two truths”: emptiness, provisional designation, and the middle, the three truths perfectly interfused, each truth containing all three. This dissolves the opposition of “verbal teaching” and “object” in the word “at once (ji).

**Position D: Yogācāra** — it matches the three natures to the two truths: the imagined nature belongs to provisional existence, the dependent nature and the perfected nature correspond respectively to the conventional and the ultimate, and it thus acknowledges that the two truths have the sense of “objects,” though the object is not apart from consciousness.

**Why this dispute matters**: the location assigned to the two truths directly determines whether “the ultimate can be spoken of” and whether “the conventional must be destroyed.” If the two truths are teaching, the conventional need not be destroyed (one does not destroy provisional designation while expressing reality); if the two truths are objects, the conventional must in the end be abandoned. The divergence of Chinese Madhyamaka, Tiantai, and Yogācāra on this point is the most economical key to understanding the differences among the Chinese Buddhist schools.

name: Dispute: Is the Tathāgatagarbha Definitive in Meaning?
aka: ru lai cang shi fou liao yi
desc:
**The question** Is the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] (the basis of Buddhahood inherent in all sentient beings) **definitive in meaning** (the final teaching) or **provisional in meaning** (an expedient teaching)?

**Position A: [[garbha_sutras|the tathāgatagarbha scriptures]]** — the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* take “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” as definitive, and say that the tathāgatagarbha is the dharma-body, is suchness released from its envelopment.

**Position B: the Yogācāra school** — the tathāgatagarbha is an expedient teaching that is “provisional in meaning”: to sentient beings who fear “non-self” and cannot arouse the aspiration, the Buddha teaches “there is a self” in order to lead them on, while the real meaning still comes back to non-self, suchness, and what is made manifest by the two emptinesses. This is the point of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*'s classification of the “three periods” — to place the tathāgatagarbha scriptures in the position of “guidance for those who can be led.”

**Position C: the Madhyamaka school** — some treatises (such as the line represented by the *Ratnagotravibhāga*) take the tathāgatagarbha and emptiness to be non-dual; other Madhyamaka masters also judge the tathāgatagarbha to be “provisional in meaning” (the Tibetan Gelug school holds precisely this position, taking the Prāsaṅgika understanding of emptiness as its criterion).

**Position D: Chinese Tiantai, Huayan, and Chan** — they take “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” as definitive, and on that basis judge Yogācāra's “five lineages” to be expedient and provisional. **Doctrinal classification here is not academic taxonomy but a declaration of school allegiance**: whether the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, or the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is ultimately definitive decides whether Buddhahood has a boundary.

**The practical consequence of the disagreement**: if there are beings without the lineage, then “universal salvation” has a theoretical boundary; if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, then the object of the bodhisattva path is infinite. This question is therefore not a metaphysical dispute that can be left in suspension — it directly determines whether the scope and the motive of practice can be without boundary.

name: The Madhyamaka–Yogācāra Controversy
aka: zhong guan yu wei shi zhi zheng
desc:
**The question** Is the “[[paratantra|dependent nature]]” real, or does it lack own-nature?

**Position A: [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]]** — the dependent nature (the dependently originated dharmas that arise in dependence on consciousness) exists; only the imagined nature superimposed upon it is nonexistent. The reason is that without the dependent nature there would be no ground for establishing “nonexistence”; and without the dependent there would be total annihilation of all dharmas.

**Position B: Madhyamaka** — the dependent nature is just dependent origination, and dependent origination is the absence of own-nature; to say that the dependent nature exists falls into the view of own-nature and contradicts “absence of own-nature.” In the ultimate sense there is neither “existence” nor “nonexistence,” and so the dependent nature cannot be established as real.

**The historical scene of the argument** In China it took concrete form as **the opposition of the Sanlun school and the Faxiang school**: the Faxiang school under Xuanzang's disciples established the “three natures” as real, the Sanlun school established that “all dharmas lack own-nature,” and the two sides argued in the early Tang over “whose classification of the three periods is definitive” (Ouyi, Daoxuan, and others also had a part in it).

**Later ways of handling it**

- **Svātantrika Madhyamaka** — since it acknowledges the conventional as existing, it can be reconciled with Yogācāra at the conventional level;
- **the Tibetan transmission** — it takes Prāsaṅgika as its criterion and judges Yogācāra to be “provisional in meaning,” yet sets Yogācāra as a necessary stage of contemplative practice within the stages of the path;
- **Chinese Tiantai and Huayan** — they do not judge who is right and who wrong but judge the two to be “each grasping one aspect of the meaning”: Tiantai encompasses both by “empty, provisional, and middle at once,” Huayan harmonises both by “true emptiness is wondrous existence.”

**Why this controversy matters** It directly determines the boundary of “emptiness”: is emptiness only the emptiness of the “imagined nature,” or does it extend so far that the “dependent nature” too has nothing to grasp? This divergence has continued into China, Tibet, and Japan, and is the most thoroughgoing dividing line in the history of Buddhist theory.

name: The Two Truths
desc:
[[conventional|conventional truth]] and [[ultimate|ultimate truth]]. Their function is neither to destroy worldly causality nor to cling to any ultimate substantial reality, thereby avoiding at once the two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.

“Truth” (satya) means “real”, but the two truths are “real” in different ways: conventional truth is “real for the world” — because the world is inverted, illusory dharmas arise, and these dharmas are real for the world; ultimate truth is “real for the noble ones” — because the noble ones truly know the nature of inversion, they know that all dharmas are empty and unborn. The two truths are therefore not two worlds but two levels of cognition with respect to one and the same set of dharmas.

Interpretations differ considerably among the schools:
- Sarvāstivāda: distinguishes “dharmas” (substantially real) from “provisional designations” (prajñapti-sat);
- Madhyamaka: the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”: “The Buddhas teach the Dharma in reliance on the two truths: one the conventional truth, the other the ultimate truth” — the two truths belong to the level of verbal teaching, and the Sanlun school goes further, using “the truth for [the world] / the truth as teaching” to state explicitly that the two truths “are only a teaching device, and have nothing to do with the object or the principle”;
- Yogācāra: the conventional is what consciousness manifests, the ultimate is suchness revealed by the two emptinesses.

The practical significance of the two truths is this: without destroying the conventional one realises the ultimate, and so one can observe the precepts, practise, and bear ethical responsibility, while clinging to no single dharma as ultimate.

name: Conventional Truth
desc:
The truth agreed upon by the world. Causality, good and evil, practice, and liberation all hold at this level.

“Conventional” (saṃvṛti) has the two senses of “covering, concealing” and “common consent, convention”: first, the cognition of ordinary beings is covered by [[ignorance|ignorance]]; second, the world takes linguistic convention as real. Conventional truth is therefore “valid but not ultimate”: within the conventional truth, killing is evil, giving is good, and causality is not deceptive; yet none of this holds as intrinsic existence.

[[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] stresses “not destroying the conventional”: precisely because without the conventional truth “the ultimate truth is not attained” — the ultimate cannot be found elsewhere, apart from the language and causality of the conventional.

name: Ultimate Truth
desc:
The ultimate truth: all dharmas are empty, without intrinsic nature, ungraspable.

“Ultimate” (paramārtha) is “the most excellent object of meaning”, referring to the object of the noble ones' wisdom. Its content is not “another, more real entity” but the fact itself that “all dharmas are without intrinsic nature”.

Ultimate truth therefore cannot be expressed positively — whatever is spoken is already conventional speech. This is why the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* (Zhong lun) uses the “eight negations” in a via negativa, and it is also where the apparent tension lies between “the real mark cannot be spoken” and “the three baskets and twelve divisions” (the latter being precisely the necessary expedient of pointing at the moon with words).

name: Emptiness
desc:
The meaning of being without intrinsic nature, and not “nothing exists”. What “emptiness” negates is only one thing: intrinsic nature (svabhāva) — a mode of existence that is not dependent on anything else, does not change, and stands independently.

The expression of emptiness is usually given in dependence on [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. The famous verse of the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* (Zhong lun), “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”, runs: “Whatever is dependently originated, that I call emptiness; it is also a provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the middle way.” The three phrases correspond respectively to: because it is dependently originated it is without intrinsic nature (emptiness); being without intrinsic nature it is provisionally designated (provisional); it falls into neither of the two extremes of existence and non-existence (middle). Emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are therefore not three stages but three facets of one and the same statement — and this too became the classical basis of the Tiantai doctrine of the three truths.

The relation between emptiness and non-self is direct: emptiness is non-self, and non-self is emptiness. The two refer to the same thing; only “emptiness” lays stress on the level of dharmas, while “non-self” lays stress on the level of persons.

name: The Three Doors of Liberation
desc:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (also rendered as non-activity, wu zuo). These are three contemplative doors entering into liberation, closely related to the [[two_truths|two truths]] and the [[three_natures|three natures]].

- The door of emptiness: contemplating all dharmas as without self and without anything belonging to a self, all dharmas being illusory and unreal;
- The door of signlessness: because of emptiness, not attaching to signs, free from all signs;
- The door of wishlessness: because of signlessness, having no craving or aspiration with respect to birth-and-death in the three realms.

The treatises make two key distinctions. First, the “three samādhis” extend to both defiled and undefiled, whereas the “three doors of liberation” are exclusively undefiled — *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushe lun), fascicle 28: “Each of these three is of two kinds, pure and undefiled … among them the undefiled ones are called the three doors of liberation, because they can serve as the entrance to nirvāṇa.” Second, the Yogācāra school establishes the three doors by way of the three natures — *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Yoga Shidi Lun), fascicle 74, establishes the door of liberation of emptiness by the imagined nature, the door of liberation of wishlessness by the dependent nature, and the door of liberation of signlessness by the perfected nature.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da Zhidu Lun), fascicle 20, uses the image that “the city of nirvāṇa has three gates”, and says: “These three doors of liberation are one dharma in the Mahāyāna; because of the cause of practice they are spoken of as three kinds” — the three doors are in fact one dharma, opened into three according to the differing faculties of sentient beings (those with much craving, those with much view, those with craving and view equally).

As to provenance it should be noted that the name “three doors of liberation” does not occur in the four Pali Nikāyas; it is a later fixed formulation. It occurs in Dharmarakṣa's translation *Fo Shuo Lishi Yi Shan Jing*, in Saṅghadeva's translation of the *Ekottara-āgama* (Zeng Yi Ahan), sūtra 8.3, and in Dānapāla's *Fo Shuo Fayin Jing*, and corresponds to sūtra 80 of the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Za Ahan Jing) and to the *Fo Shuo Sheng Fayin Jing* — the latter being precisely the possible source of the name “three seals of the Dharma”.

src.q: Through the three contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and nothingness, one finally contemplates [[anatta|non-self]] and nothing belonging to a self, thereby abandoning the habit of conceit and attaining purity of knowledge and vision; this is called the “seal of the noble Dharma”.
“Among them the undefiled ones are called the [[three_doors|three doors of liberation]], because they can serve as the entrance to nirvāṇa.”

“The real mark of all dharmas is the city of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]], and the city has three gates: emptiness, signlessness, and non-activity.” “In the Mahāyāna it is one dharma; because of the cause of practice it is spoken of as three kinds.”

name: The Three Natures
desc:
The structure of delusion and awakening in [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] (Yogācāra): the [[parikalpita|imagined nature]], the dependent nature, and the perfected nature. The three are not three worlds but three cognitive states with respect to one and the same dependently originated dharma.

Their relation is as follows:
- The dependent nature — all dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this is the actual level of existence;
- The imagined nature — falsely grasping the dharmas of the dependent nature as possessing independent intrinsic nature; this belongs to “delusion”;
- The perfected nature — on the basis of the dependent nature, being free from the imagined nature and realising the suchness revealed by the two emptinesses; this belongs to “awakening”.

Hence within the three natures the dependent nature is the pivot: neither delusion nor awakening is apart from it, the difference lying only in whether grasping has arisen upon it. The correspondence with the two truths is: the imagined nature is provisional existence, the dependent nature is conventional existence, the perfected nature is ultimate existence.

The three natures are also the basis on which the three doors of liberation are established (see *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74); this group of concepts therefore runs through Yogācāra ontology, epistemology, and soteriology at once.

name: The Imagined Nature
desc:
Falsely grasping the dharmas of the dependent nature as possessing independent intrinsic nature; this is the side of “delusion”. “Imagining” (parikalpa) means “conceiving everywhere” — the mind measures and grasps universally with respect to all dharmas, taking them as existent with intrinsic nature.

Its characteristic is “affirmed in sentient experience but absent in reality” (qing you li wu): it genuinely exists in the cognition of sentient beings (affirmed in sentient experience), but it does not exist in the actual dharmas (non-existent in principle). It is therefore not “yet another thing” but “an error”.

This distinction is the key to how [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] deals with “delusion”: delusion is not an extra layer of world, but a misreading of the world that is already there.

src.q: “The imagined nature is affirmed in sentient experience but absent in reality.”

src.t: *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Jie Shenmi Jing), “Chapter on the Marks of All Dharmas” (Yi Qie Fa Xiang Pin)

tt.fix: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659)

name: The Dependent Nature
desc:
All dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this belongs to the level of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. “Dependent on others” (paratantra) means “arising in dependence on other conditions” — not autonomous, not independent, entirely constituted by conditions.

The dependent nature is the pivot among the [[three_natures|three natures]] and also the focus of the most concentrated discussion between Yogācāra and Madhyamaka: Madhyamaka holds that the dependent nature is synonymous with dependent origination, that is, “without intrinsic nature”; Yogācāra, by contrast, diverges from Madhyamaka in acknowledging the dependent nature as “truly existent” (the dependent nature exists; it is only that the imagined nature does not exist upon it).

Within the Yogācāra system the dependent nature corresponds directly to “consciousness” — since it appears in dependence on consciousness, the dependent nature is what consciousness transforms.

src.q: “The dependent nature is real in principle but non-existent in deluded sentient experience” — the dependent nature has its own distinct substantiality, unlike the imagined nature, which is wholly non-existent.
It takes the dependent nature as “the nature of discrimination” (vikalpa-svabhāva).

name: The Perfected Nature
desc:
Being free from the imagined nature on the basis of the dependent nature, and realising the [[suchness|suchness]] revealed by the two emptinesses (the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas); this is the side of “awakening”.

“Consummate” means complete, “accomplished” means achieved, “real” means true. It is not a new thing that needs to be produced, but the actual state revealed on the dependent nature once false grasping has been removed. The practice of [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] is therefore not “acquisition” but “turning away and turning toward” (zhuan she zhuan de) — what is discarded is the imagined nature, what is obtained is the perfected nature.

The perfected nature is suchness, namely the unconditioned of suchness among the six unconditioned dharmas, and it is the ultimate truth of consciousness-only.

src.t: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-only), fascicles 8 and 9
src.q: “The real nature of all dharmas, consummate and accomplished, revealed by the two emptinesses, is called the [[chengshi|perfected]] nature.”

tt.fix: *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659)

name: The Eight Consciousnesses
desc:
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]]. The first six consciousnesses discern coarse objects, manas constantly examines and deliberates, and ālaya-consciousness retains the seeds and receives perfuming.

How the doctrine of the eight consciousnesses came to be established: the first five consciousnesses are sensory cognition; the sixth, mind-consciousness, synthesises and discerns, and also takes past and future as its objects; the seventh, manas, constantly and persistently considers the eighth consciousness as “I”, and is the direct source of self-grasping; the eighth, ālaya, contains all seeds, becomes manifest when conditions obtain, and performs the function of being the vehicle of the [[continuity|continuity]] of karma.

The significance of this system lies in solving the technical problem of “rebirth without a self”: there is no need to posit a substantial soul, yet one must explain how karma continues across lives — ālaya-consciousness performs precisely this function by way of “the continuity of consciousness” rather than “the transmigration of a substance”.

name: Ālaya-consciousness
desc:
The [[eight_consciousnesses|eighth consciousness]], which contains all seeds and becomes manifest when conditions obtain; it is the vehicle of the [[continuity|continuity]] of karma and of the continuation of life. “Ālaya” means “storehouse” and has three senses: the store (neng cang, that which can contain the seeds of all dharmas), the stored (suo cang, that which is perfumed by all dharmas and is their basis), and the storehouse of appropriation (zhi cang, that which is grasped as “I” by manas).

Its operation is described as “constantly turning like a violent torrent”: it arises and perishes moment by moment yet continues without interruption, neither permanent nor annihilated. This simile answers two errors at once: taking it as permanent (which would make it a substantial self), and taking it as annihilated (which would leave the fruits of karma without an owner).

The tathāgatagarbha tradition offers another reading: the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* (Ru Lengqie Jing), fascicle 7, says, “The ālaya-consciousness is called the tathāgatagarbha, and is together with the seven consciousnesses of ignorance” — this equates ālaya-consciousness with the tathāgatagarbha, bringing the “consciousness” of Yogācāra and the “mind-nature” of the tathāgatagarbha tradition into convergence in later Indian and Chinese Buddhist thought.

name: Transformation of Consciousness into Wisdom
desc:
The core of “transformation of the basis”: turning away from the defiled and turning toward the pure. “Transformation of consciousness into wisdom” means that the [[eight_consciousnesses|eight consciousnesses]] are transformed into the [[four_wisdoms|four wisdoms]]; it is the ultimate goal of Yogācāra.

In “transformation of the basis” (āśraya-parāvṛtti) the “basis” (āśraya) means that which is relied upon — ālaya-consciousness and all its seeds. Transformation of the basis does not mean that the substance of the mind changes, but that the “basis” of consciousness turns from defiled to pure: the eighth consciousness becomes the great mirror wisdom, the seventh becomes the wisdom of equality, the sixth becomes the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the first five become the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

The key lies in the word “transformation”: it is not the annihilation of consciousness and the creation of another wisdom, but the transformation of the same function once grasping has been relinquished. This is structurally akin to Madhyamaka's “afflictions are themselves enlightenment” and Tiantai's “a single moment of ignorance is the mind of the Dharma-nature”, though Yogācāra preserves a more detailed account of the stages and the mechanism.

src.q: The sequence and correlation by which the [[eight_consciousnesses|eight consciousnesses]] are transformed into the four wisdoms.

name: Tathāgatagarbha
desc:
The basis for attaining Buddhahood that all sentient beings intrinsically possess; that is, [[pure_mind|the intrinsically pure mind]] and [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]], merely covered by ignorance and not yet manifest. The literal meaning of “tathāgatagarbha” (ru lai zang) is “the Tathāgata in the womb” — the Tathāgata is present in potency within the bodies of sentient beings.

It provides the ontological basis for attaining Buddhahood and explains the mechanism of delusion and awakening: the mind-nature is intrinsically pure, but is defiled by adventitious dust. Delusion and awakening are therefore not a difference between “having” and “not having” but between “covered” and “manifest”.

“Garbha” has three senses (*Buddha-nature Treatise*, Fo Xing Lun, fascicle 2, “Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha”):
- the garbha as that which is encompassed: all sentient beings are encompassed within the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
- the garbha as concealment: the dharma-body does not change in either the causal or the fruition stage, yet sentient beings cannot see it because they are covered by affliction;
- the garbha as that which encompasses: the qualities of the Tathāgata's fruition are entirely encompassed within the minds of ordinary beings.

This page situates the concept in the line of inquiry concerned with the “basis for attaining Buddhahood” — namely: once non-self has been established, the subjective ground for Buddhahood can only fall on the mind-nature itself. This placement is not, however, the consensus of all schools: Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka does not accept a truly existent tathāgatagarbha (for fear of falling into eternalism), nor does Yogācāra wholly equate its own position with the tathāgatagarbha; Chinese Tiantai, Huayan, and Chan, by contrast, absorbed it extensively and made it central to their doctrinal classification.

src.q: By nine similes — a transformed Buddha within a lotus, pure honey in a rock-tree, true gold fallen into an impure place, a golden image wrapped in worthless cloth, a lowly woman bearing a noble child, and so on — it explains that the Tathāgata is intrinsically present within the bodies of sentient beings. It is generally regarded as the earliest [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] scripture to appear.

name: Buddha-nature
desc:
The possibility of awakening and the ultimate basis that sentient beings intrinsically possess. “Buddha-nature”, [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]], [[pure_mind|the intrinsically pure mind]], the dharma-nature, suchness, and the real mark are concepts that are “one in meaning though different in name”.

There is one important divergence between the Indian Buddhist doctrine of “lineage” (gotra) and the Chinese doctrine of “Buddha-nature”: Indian Yogācāra posits the “five lineages” (the śrāvaka lineage, the pratyekabuddha lineage, the bodhisattva lineage, the indeterminate lineage, and the lineage-less), maintaining that sentient beings of the “lineage-less” kind can never attain Buddhahood; whereas the position of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* that “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature” became the basis for the consensus of Chinese Buddhist thought that “all can attain Buddhahood”.

This divergence has considerable practical consequences: if there are lineage-less sentient beings, then “universal salvation” has a theoretical limit; if all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, then the scope of the bodhisattva path is infinite. Both Tiantai and Huayan adopt the latter.

src.q: “All sentient beings possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”; it uses gold in ore as a simile.

name: The Intrinsically Pure Mind
desc:
The mind-nature is intrinsically pure, but is defiled by adventitious dust. Delusion and awakening are therefore not the acquisition of something new, but the removal of a covering.

The thesis that “the mind-nature is intrinsically pure” (Pali pabhassara-citta) already appears in the Āgamas and the schools: the mind is defiled by adventitious dust and affliction, yet the nature of the mind is pure. The schools differed on this — the [[sarvastivada|Sarvāstivāda]] and others held that “the mind-nature is intrinsically pure” refers to “the possibility that the mind will attain Buddhahood in the future” rather than to “being pure right now”.

In the [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] tradition, the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra*'s “the intrinsically pure mind, defiled by adventitious dust and affliction” became the standard formulation. “Adventitious dust” combines two images, “adventitious” (a temporary guest, not a permanent resident) and “dust” (an external accretion). Adventitious dust is thus the imagined nature — what covers the mind-nature is grasping, not the mind-nature itself.

This structure makes practice a matter of “removing the covering” rather than “fabricating”: there is no need to produce a pure mind, only to remove the obscuration. Chan's “illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature” and Tiantai's “a single moment of ignorance is the mind of the Dharma-nature” both inherit this.

name: The Bodhisattva Path
desc:
The core path of the Mahāyāna: arousing the mind of enlightenment, practising the [[six_paramitas|six pāramitās]], traversing the ten stages, and attaining Buddhahood in order to save sentient beings. It is the direction in which [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]] thought unfolds within Mahāyāna practice.

The key to the bodhisattva path lies in the “mind of enlightenment” (bodhicitta) — the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings. This motive transforms practice from “seeking one's own liberation” into “liberation together with all sentient beings”, and on this ground the Mahāyāna criticises the śrāvaka vehicle as “self-serving”.

As to stages, the bodhisattva path comprises the ten stages (from the stage of Joy to the stage of the Dharma-cloud), coordinated with the ten pāramitās, and Buddhahood is attained after three great incalculable aeons. Huayan, Yogācāra, and Tiantai each have their own detailed assessment of the ten stages.

The point of connection between tathāgatagarbha thought and the bodhisattva path is this: since all sentient beings intrinsically possess the tathāgatagarbha, “saving sentient beings” is not the bestowal of something out of nothing but the helping of sentient beings to remove their covering and bring out what they intrinsically possess — this gives the bodhisattva path an inner necessity rather than making it a merely external command.

name: The Six Pāramitās
desc:
Giving, observance of precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Also called the six pāramitās; “pāramitā” means “gone to the other shore” — by these six one can go from this shore of birth-and-death to the other shore of [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]].

The inner sequence of the six: giving first counteracts stinginess and greed; observance of precepts establishes a norm of conduct; patience keeps the first two unbroken in adverse circumstances; diligence keeps them uninterrupted; meditative concentration concentrates the power of the mind; wisdom keeps the first five from falling into grasping, so that they become “pāramitās” and not merely human and heavenly merit.

The treatises further speak of “cultivating the six pāramitās through three matters” — only when the six are combined with the three matters of “attention concomitant with the wisdom of omniscience, great compassion as the foremost, and non-acquisition as the expedient means” do they become the [[bodhisattva_path|bodhisattva path]] rather than mere virtuous action. This account makes the six pāramitās inseparable from the emptiness-wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā.

name: Sanlun (Madhyamaka)
desc:
The school is founded on the three treatises — the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* — and belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā and [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] tradition. Its core is dependent origination and intrinsic emptiness, the middle way of the eight negations, the two truths, and non-attainment. Its ultimate aim is to realise the true reality of the middle way and enter the non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Its distinguishing feature is “refuting without establishing”: it demolishes layer by layer by way of the apophatic method (negation) and establishes no affirmative proposition, and therefore asserts no thesis of its own, saying only that “in refuting the false, the true is revealed.” In its doctrine of the two truths it holds to “the two truths as verbal teaching” — the two truths are the form of the Buddha's preaching, not the principle that is realised or the object that is contemplated.

Lineage: in India, Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250) → Āryadeva → transmitted to China through Kumārajīva (401) → Sengquan of Sheshan and Falang of Xinghuang → Jizang (549–623), who brought it to completion.

name: The Eight Negations
aka: middle way of the eight negations
desc:
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, [[not_one_not_diff|neither one nor different]], neither coming nor going (Kumārajīva renders it “neither coming nor departing”). The middle way is revealed by way of negation (the apophatic method), avoiding any extreme.

The eight negations come from the salutation verse at the opening of the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* and form the general outline of the whole work. Their structure is four pairs: arising and ceasing (existence and non-existence), permanence and annihilation, identity and difference, coming and going. The four pairs address respectively whether existence arises, whether time continues, whether identity holds, and whether motion is possible — that is, the four most basic types of attachment to “dharmas” both within Buddhism and among non-Buddhists.

The methodological significance of the eight negations is that they do not state the truth positively but reveal the middle way by showing that “this path does not lead through.” Madhyamaka is therefore called “refuting without establishing.” This method deeply influenced Tiantai, though Tiantai placed limits on its use and did not go to the Chan-style extreme.

src.q: “Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither one nor different, neither coming nor departing. He who teaches dependent origination, who well extinguishes all conceptual proliferation.”

name: Non-attainment and Non-abiding Nirvāṇa
desc:
Not grasping that any dharma is attainable; not abiding in birth-and-death (saṃsāra), nor abiding in [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]].

“Non-attainment” (anupalambha) is the practical principle of the [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] and Prajñāpāramitā traditions: if there is something attained, there is something grasped; if there is grasping, there can be no true liberation. Hence even “nirvāṇa” cannot be taken as an object to be attained.

Relation to Chan: the “non-abiding” of the Ox-head school and of Southern Chan shares this same source — the *Platform Sūtra* (Liuzu Tan Jing) takes “non-abiding as the root,” that is, not lingering over any dharma, which is structurally identical with “non-attainment.” The Sanlun school's “non-attainment” and Chan's “non-abiding” are thus the same principle expressed in different schools.

“Non-abiding nirvāṇa” is the Mahāyāna redefinition of nirvāṇa: unlike the hearers' “entering nirvāṇa and stopping there,” the bodhisattva, out of great compassion, does not abide in nirvāṇa, and, out of wisdom, does not abide in saṃsāra. This formulation turns nirvāṇa from an “endpoint” into a “state of non-attachment.”

name: Faxiang (Yogācāra)
desc:
The school is founded on the *[[doc_5|Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra]]*, the *[[doc_32|Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra]]*, and the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, and represents the transmission in China of the Indian Yogācāra tradition. Its core is the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the transformation of the basis, and the four wisdoms. Its ultimate aim is to cut off the two obstructions (the affliction obstruction and the cognitive obstruction), realise the two emptinesses (the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas), transform consciousness into wisdom, and attain the three bodies of the Buddha.

Its distinguishing feature is the detailed analysis of dharma-characteristics: by means of precise classifications such as the five categories and one hundred dharmas and the fifty-one mental factors, it explains the constitution and causal relations of all dharmas, and is the most systematically philosophical of Buddhist systems. To the difficult problem of “non-self yet rebirth” it gives the most technical answer — ālaya-consciousness holds the seeds and receives perfuming, constantly turning like a torrent, neither permanent nor annihilated.

Lineage: in India, Asaṅga (c. 310–390) and Vasubandhu (c. 320–400) → Paramārtha (came to China in the 6th century; the Shelun masters) → Xuanzang (returned to China in 645; translated the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in 646–648; the *Cheng Weishi Lun* was completed in 659) → Kuiji.

Because it holds that among the “five lineages” there is one class of sentient beings who can never attain Buddhahood, it conflicts with the position of Tiantai, Huayan, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.” Accordingly its doctrinal classification ranks the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* as the definitive meaning of the third period, while judging the *Lotus* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as provisional meaning prior to the “three periods” — this classificatory stance is precisely one of the greatest disagreements within Chinese Buddhist learning.

src.q: The scriptural source for the doctrine of the [[three_natures|three natures]] and of ālaya-consciousness.
The classification of the [[five_paths|five categories]] and one hundred dharmas, and the argument establishing ālaya-consciousness.
Compiled by conflating the commentaries of ten masters; the culminating work of [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] learning.

name: Tiantai
desc:
The school is founded on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Its core is [[one_mind_3000|three thousand realms in a single moment of mind]], the perfect interfusion of the three truths, threefold contemplation in one mind, and the [[six_identities|six identities]]. Its characteristic is to begin from the single moment of mind of the ordinary person, giving equal weight to doctrine and contemplation, with clear stages. Its ultimate aim is to open the Buddha's insight, perfectly realise true reality, and become the Buddha of the ultimate identity.

The structure of its thought is that “the perfect interfusion of the three truths” and “three thousand realms in a single moment of mind” support each other: the three truths explain the mode in which the mind is contemplated (empty, provisional, and middle at once), while three thousand realms in a single moment of mind explains the content of the mind (a single moment of mind suffices for the three thousand worlds). Their combination makes Tiantai the Chinese school most characterised by “perfect interfusion” — it does not divide phenomenon and noumenon into two levels, but says that every colour and every fragrance possesses the three thousand.

In doctrinal classification it takes the *Lotus Sūtra* as purely perfect and uniquely sublime, and the five periods and eight teachings rank the earlier sūtras as provisional teachings. Compared with Huayan: Huayan directly reveals the realm of the Buddha's fruit and is grand in scale; Tiantai begins from the single moment of mind of the ordinary person, with clear stages and strong practicability.

Lineage: Huiwen → Huisi → Zhiyi (538–597) → Guanding (who recorded and edited his works). Zhiyi's major works — the *Fahua Xuanyi*, the *Fahua Wenju*, and the *Mohe Zhiguan* — were all recorded by his disciple Guanding from his lectures.

name: Three Thousand Realms in a Single Moment of Mind
aka: three thousand worlds in one thought
desc:
A single moment of mind contains in full the three thousand worlds. The classic statement in fascicle 5 of the *[[doc_39|Mohe Zhiguan]]*: “Now, one mind contains the ten dharma-realms, and one dharma-realm in turn contains the ten dharma-realms, [making] a hundred dharma-realms; one realm contains thirty kinds of world, so a hundred dharma-realms contain three thousand kinds of world. These three thousand are in a single moment of mind: if there is no mind, that is all; but as soon as there is the slightest mind, it contains the three thousand.”

The calculation of the three thousand: the ten dharma-realms (the six ordinary realms plus the four noble realms) × the ten dharma-realms (each realm again containing the ten realms) = a hundred dharma-realms; a hundred dharma-realms × the ten suchnesses (characteristic, nature, substance, power, activity, cause, condition, effect, retribution, and the ultimate equality of beginning and end) = a thousand suchnesses; a thousand suchnesses × the three kinds of world (the world of the five aggregates, the world of sentient beings, and the world of the land) = the three thousand worlds.

The key lies in the relation between “a single moment” and “the three thousand.” The *Mohe Zhiguan* states explicitly: “It is not said that one mind comes first and all dharmas afterwards; nor is it said that all dharmas come first and one mind afterwards” — it is not that the mind generates the three thousand (vertically), nor that the mind contains the three thousand all at once (horizontally), but that “the mind alone is all dharmas, and all dharmas are the mind.” “The three thousand” is therefore a synonym for “all dharmas,” and one need not fixate on the number; its essential spirit is “inherent inclusion” — the ordinary person's present single moment of mind is already complete in possessing everything, with no need to seek outside.

The scriptural basis of the doctrine is the *[[doc_12|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]*, “Chapter on the Sovereignty of the Yāma Heaven Palace”: “Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction”; but “three thousand realms in a single moment of mind” itself is a contemplation unique to Tiantai.

src.q: “These three thousand are in a single moment of mind: if there is no mind, that is all; but as soon as there is the slightest mind, it contains the three thousand. It is not said that one mind comes first and all dharmas afterwards; nor is it said that all dharmas come first and one mind afterwards.”

name: Perfect Interfusion of the Three Truths and Threefold Contemplation in One Mind
aka: perfect interfusion of the three truths
round fusion of the three truths
desc:
The three truths — emptiness, the provisional, and the middle — are not three successive stages but are perfectly illumined at once within one mind.

The scriptural basis for the three truths is the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]*, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”: “Whatever dharma arises from causes and conditions, I declare to be emptiness; it is also a provisional name, and is also called the meaning of the middle way.” The three phrases are the three truths of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Zhiyi's crucial treatment is “the mutual identity of the three truths”: the three — emptiness, provisional, middle — are “neither one nor three, yet one and yet three” — not three independent truths, but the simultaneous presentation of the same true reality from different angles.

“Threefold contemplation in one mind” is the corresponding contemplation: within one mind to contemplate emptiness, the provisional, and the middle simultaneously, without having to cultivate the three contemplations in stages. This stands in contrast to the “successive threefold contemplation” of the distinct teaching, and is the mark by which Tiantai judges the “perfect teaching.”

The relation of the three truths to the [[two_truths|two truths]]: the three truths are opened out from the two truths, and the three truths are the two truths — because the “middle” is not a third truth apart from the two truths, but the perfectly interfused aspect of the two truths. Tiantai therefore says, “the two truths open into the three truths, and the three truths are the two truths.”

Comparison with the Sanlun school: Sanlun discusses the middle way on the basis of the “eight negations” in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and sets it forth in conjunction with the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional; Tiantai, on the other hand, establishes the perfectly interfused three truths on the basis of the verse in the “Examination of the Four Noble Truths” chapter, so that Tiantai's view of the middle way carries more of a sense of “the perfectly interfused phenomenal realm” — “empty, provisional, and middle at once” affirms at the same time the validity of provisional names.

name: Opening the Buddha's Insight
desc:
The cardinal teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*: opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha's insight.

The sūtra says that the sole great cause for the Buddha's appearance in the world is to lead sentient beings to “open the Buddha's insight, show the Buddha's insight, awaken to the Buddha's insight, and enter the Buddha's insight.” Tiantai takes this as the reason for judging the *Lotus* to be purely perfect — the *Lotus* sets forth no expedient device apart from opening the provisional to reveal the real, but speaks only of the Buddha's true intent.

“Opening” has a double meaning: first, “opening away,” that is, removing sentient beings' attachment to provisional teachings; second, “opening up,” that is, revealing the Buddha's insight that is inherently possessed. “Opening the Buddha's insight” therefore corresponds structurally to “all sentient beings possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”: the insight is not added from outside but is inherently possessed and obscured.

Relation to the “[[six_identities|six identities]]”: “opening the Buddha's insight” is the cardinal teaching of the doctrinal classification, while the “six identities” are the stages of practice; the former explains the nature of the goal, the latter the position of attainment.

src.q: “The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause ... wishing to lead sentient beings to [[kaifozhijian|open the Buddha's insight]], show the Buddha's insight, awaken to the Buddha's insight, and enter the Buddha's insight.”
